0.title: The Magna Carta of Christian Liberty: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
0.overview:
Paul wrote to the Galatians in a state of controlled fury. He was angry not for himself but for them — and for the gospel. Every other letter he wrote to a church opens with thanksgiving or blessing to God; Galatians has neither. He moves immediately, in the very first verse, to defend his apostolic authority, and by verse 6 he is in open astonishment: “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel.” The urgency that presses through every paragraph of this letter was born of Paul’s conviction that the gospel itself was at stake — not a peripheral issue but the very core of what he had preached and what they had received.

The crisis had been created by a group scholars call the Judaizers — Jewish Christians who insisted that faith in Christ was necessary but not sufficient. Gentile believers also needed to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic law in order to be fully accepted by God and fully included in God’s people. This seems, on the surface, like a minor addition: faith in Christ plus a few religious practices. But Paul saw it with total clarity for what it was: a fundamental contradiction of the gospel. If anything in addition to Christ is required for justification — even something God-given and ancient like circumcision — then Christ is no longer sufficient, grace is no longer free, and the cross is no longer enough. “If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21).

Where were these churches, and when did Paul write? Galatia was both an ethnic region in the north of Asia Minor, settled by Celtic tribes, and a Roman province that also took in the southern cities of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Some think Paul wrote to ethnic Galatians in the north, whom he may have visited on his later journeys (Acts 16:6; 18:23), and date the letter in the mid-50s. The more likely reading is that he wrote to the southern churches he founded on his first journey (Acts 13–14): Paul normally used the Roman provincial names, and Acts tells us plainly about those churches and nothing about any in the north. On that reading the letter was written around AD 48, just before the Jerusalem Council, which would explain why Paul never mentions the Council’s decision (cf. 2:1). It may well be his earliest letter. Its message does not depend on the answer.

Galatians is structured in three movements. Chapters 1–2 are autobiographical: Paul defends the divine origin of his gospel (he received it not from men but from Jesus Christ directly) and recounts his confrontation with Peter at Antioch, where the gospel’s logic was at stake in a table-fellowship dispute. Chapters 3–4 are theological: Paul argues from Scripture (Abraham, the covenant, the law’s purpose, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah) that the gospel of grace by faith preceded the Mosaic law by 430 years and is not superseded by it. Chapters 5–6 are practical: the freedom of the gospel is not license for the flesh but the only true basis for life in the Spirit and love for the neighbor.

Martin Luther’s Commentary on Galatians (1535) is among the most celebrated commentaries in the history of the church. He called this letter his “Katie von Bora” — his beloved, the one he was married to. For Luther, Galatians was the text that articulated what the Reformation was about: the righteousness of God is not a demanding standard to be met but a free gift to be received. Justification is by faith alone, in Christ alone, by grace alone. Anything added to that formula is a subtraction from it.

Read Galatians as the most passionate defense of free grace in the entire canon. Every person who has ever felt that their standing before God depends on their performance needs to hear it. Every church that has drifted toward moralism — toward making the Christian life about spiritual self-improvement rather than trust in the finished work of Christ — needs to be dragged back to Galatians and made to sit with it until the gospel is clear again. Paul wrote it because the gospel is always under threat, and the threat almost always comes from the same direction: the desire to add something to Christ, to make grace a little less free, to make human effort a little more decisive. Galatians says: no. The cross is enough. Christ is enough. Grace is enough. “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

1.title: No Other Gospel: The Divine Origin of Paul’s Message
1.overview:
The letter begins with a defense of apostolic authority and immediately escalates to a declaration that would have shocked its first hearers: the gospel Paul preached is not of human origin, and anyone — even an angel from heaven — who preaches a different gospel is under divine curse. The word translated “accursed” is anathema — the strongest possible language of divine condemnation. Paul uses it twice in two verses (vv. 8–9), the repetition signaling that this is not rhetorical heat but deliberate, settled conviction.

The reason for the severity is simple: if the gospel can be modified by human authority — by apostles, by tradition, by ecclesiastical consensus — then it is not the gospel of God but the gospel of men. And the gospel of men, however sincerely presented, however religiously decorated, cannot save. Only the gospel that comes from God can bring a person into right standing with God. The divine origin of the gospel is therefore not an abstract theological claim; it is the practical ground of the gospel’s saving power.

Paul then makes his case autobiographically. He was not taught the gospel by the Jerusalem apostles; he received it directly from Jesus Christ, by revelation. The account of his conversion and his minimal contact with the Jerusalem church in the years that followed is not self-congratulation but an argument: his gospel is independently and divinely authenticated. It is the same gospel the Jerusalem apostles preach — but its authority does not rest on their endorsement. It rests on the revelation of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens by stressing that his apostleship came not from any human source or appointment but directly from Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, the very point his opponents in Galatia disputed. Writing with the believers around him to the churches of Galatia, he wishes them grace and peace from God and from Christ, who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, as the Father willed, and he gives glory to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as Eternal Initiative, Not Emergency Repair

The christological formula of vv. 3–5 is among the earliest in the New Testament, and it grounds the Reformed conviction that salvation originates wholly in God. The Son’s self-giving is voluntary; its object is our sins; its effect is rescue out of an age, not improvement within it; and its source is the Father’s own will. Two errors are shut out at once. The first makes the cross a late correction to a plan that went wrong — but Christ gave himself according to the will of our God and Father, and Peter preaches the same thing at Pentecost, that he was delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

The second sets a stern Father against a merciful Son, as though mercy had to be extracted from heaven by the death of Jesus. Verse 4 forbids it. The Father willed the giving; the Son gave himself; there is no division of sentiment in the Trinity toward sinners. Grace is not reactive. It is eternal initiative, and it terminates in glory to God (v. 5), which is where the letter will end up as well.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had received a complete gospel and were being told it was a foundation needing a second storey. Paul’s opening answers that before it is raised: the apostleship is unmediated (v. 1), the senders are a company and not a maverick (v. 2), and the gospel summarised in vv. 3–5 has no vacancy in it for a human contribution — Christ gave himself, and the Father willed it.

Now: The same instinct survives wherever the gospel is treated as the entry requirement and something else as the real content of the Christian life — a sacramental record, a moral achievement, an intensity of spiritual experience. The test is simple and can be run on a bad week: if approaching God after a week of failure feels materially different from approaching him after a good one, something has already been added, whatever is said out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead— and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s authority and his gospel come directly from the risen Christ and God the Father, not from any human source.

Not from men nor through man. His opponents said Paul was a second-hand apostle, dependent on Jerusalem. He answers in the first line.

Who raised him. Paul was commissioned by the risen Lord (Acts 9:15).

The churches of Galatia. Where scholars differ. The North Galatian view sees ethnic Galatians in central Asia Minor, evangelised on Paul’s second journey. The South Galatian view sees the Roman province, including Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13–14), which would make this possibly Paul’s earliest letter, written before the Jerusalem council (Acts 15). Verdict: the South Galatian view, with an early date, best explains why Paul does not mention the council’s decision.

No thanksgiving. Unique among Paul’s letters: the situation is too serious.
verseByVerse.note: Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor. Many think the letter went to the churches Paul founded on his first journey — Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe; others think of ethnic Galatians farther north.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart of the gospel is in the greeting: Christ gave himself for our sins to rescue us from this evil age, all by the Father’s will and for his glory.

Gave himself for our sins. Substitution: our sins required his death (1 Corinthians 15:3).

To deliver us. Rescue from the present evil age, its powers and its condemnation.

According to the will of God. The cross was the Father’s plan, not an accident.

For worship. If Christ gave himself for your sins, nothing need be added. Glory to God for ever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Instead of thanksgiving, Paul expresses astonishment that the Galatians are so quickly turning from the God who called them by grace to a different gospel, which is no gospel at all, only a distortion spread by people unsettling them. Anyone who preaches a gospel contrary to the one they received, even Paul himself or an angel, is under God’s curse; he says it twice. He is not trying to win human approval; if he were, he would not be Christ’s servant.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Stands Over the Church That Preaches It

The double anathema of vv. 8–9 establishes something the Reformers staked their lives on: the gospel is not the church’s property, to be developed by councils or refined by consensus. A message that human authority conferred can be amended by human authority, and would be. Paul therefore submits himself and heaven’s own courier to the same test he asks the Galatians to apply, which is not the prestige of the teacher but conformity to what was first delivered. Luther read these two verses and recognised the whole controversy of his century in them.

It should be added, because Paul’s own practice requires it, that the curse is not aimed at every disagreement among Christians: he allows real latitude on food and days and disputable matters (Rom. 14). What cannot be renegotiated is the ground of acceptance with God. And the reason nobody may edit this gospel is that it was bought, not drafted — there was an anathema in this story before Paul used the word, and it fell on the Son, becoming a curse for us (3:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were very probably sincere, and would have described themselves as the conservative party taking the Old Testament seriously. Circumcision was God’s own ordinance; the law was divinely given. They were not conscious apostates but well-meaning teachers who had inverted the relationship of law and grace — which is exactly why v. 10 matters, since sincerity was never the test.

Now: A different gospel rarely announces itself as one. It presents as the fuller, more serious, more culturally credible version. Two questions from this passage sort it out. Does this teaching change the ground on which a sinner is accepted by God, or only a secondary matter Christians have long disagreed about? And for a reader with a mother or a brother in such a church, the pastoral answer is in the grammar of vv. 8–9: the anathema falls on the one preaching, not on the sheep being misled.

verseByVerse.quote: I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To turn from the gospel of grace to another message is to desert God himself, and that other message is no gospel at all.

Astonished. Paul cannot believe how quickly they have turned.

Deserting him. Not merely a doctrine but a person, the God who called them by grace.

A different gospel. The agitators taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law to be fully accepted (5:2–4; 6:12). Adding anything to Christ empties the gospel.

Trouble you. They disturb and distort.

On a Tuesday. Watch for “Jesus plus” in your own heart: Jesus plus my performance, my tradition, my experience.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers had come insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel is so fixed that even an apostle or an angel who changed it would stand under God’s curse.

Even we. The message judges the messenger, not the other way round.

Accursed. Anathema: devoted to destruction. Paul says it twice.

What it does not mean. Not that every disagreement is anathema, but that changing the way of salvation, grace through faith in Christ alone, is fatal.

Where Christians differ. Some use this verse to condemn all who differ on secondary matters; others think doctrinal boundaries are unloving. Verdict: the gospel of justification by grace through faith is a first-order truth worth this solemnity; on secondary matters, charity.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema — handed over to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant of Christ cannot also be a people-pleaser.

Approval of man or God? His opponents probably said Paul dropped circumcision to make the gospel easier.

Servant. Doulos, slave: one master only.

On a Tuesday. Whose approval are you seeking today? You cannot serve Christ and live for applause.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now argues from his own biography, and the argument is chronological. In vv. 11–12 he states the thesis: the gospel he preached is not man’s gospel; he did not receive it from any man, nor was he taught it. Those two verbs are the exact vocabulary of rabbinic transmission, the machinery that had made him a Pharisee, and he is saying it had nothing to do with this. (When he tells Corinth that he received and delivered the resurrection facts, there is no contradiction: the facts came from the church, the meaning and the commission came by revelation of Jesus Christ.)

Then the evidence. Verses 13–14 are his own record of shame produced as an exhibit: he persecuted the church beyond measure and tried to destroy it, the verb an army uses of a city it means to leave uninhabitable — and he was advancing beyond his peers, ahead of many of his own age, winning at the system he was in. Nobody defects from the top of a religion he is succeeding at into a message that gets him flogged. In vv. 15–16 the sentence turns and every verb becomes God’s: set me apart before I was born (before there was a person there to be good or bad), called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son — God’s delight, not his duty — and the commission to the Gentiles arrives in the same breath as the conversion.

The rest is a chronology of distance. Verse 17 has him going not to Jerusalem but to Arabia, the Nabatean kingdom, where he was evidently preaching hard enough to make an enemy of a king (2 Cor. 11:32–33). Verses 18–19 give the numbers that carry the argument: after three years, fifteen days, two men — and the verb translated visit means to get to know someone, not to be trained or certified by them.

Verse 20 breaks off into an oath, which tells us Paul was not merely disagreed with but called a liar. Verses 21–22 put him in Syria and Cilicia — home to Tarsus, and several years with nothing recorded — still unknown in person, literally unknown by face, to the very Judean churches he had once hunted. And vv. 23–24 close with the one sentence those churches kept repeating: he who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy. Their response was not to check his credentials. They glorified God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Effectual Calling, and Revelation: the Grammar of Grace

Verses 15–16 are among the most compact statements of sovereign grace in Paul. Three divine acts stand in order, and Paul initiates none of them: God set him apart before birth, called him by grace, and was pleased to reveal his Son in him. The setting apart echoes Jeremiah called before the womb and the Servant of Isaiah 49; there may also be a deliberate play on words, since aphorizō, to set apart, sounds against the name Pharisee, most likely from a root meaning the separated ones.

Paul had separated himself by rigorous effort and it made him dangerous; God had set him apart before he separated himself from anything, and set him apart for the Gentiles. The calling is effectual, not an invitation awaiting a reply — the last thing Saul intended on that road was conversion. And the revelation is in me, internal as well as external: he had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Grace that reaches a man riding in the opposite direction with warrants in his bag is not a reward for seeking. (cf. Rom. 8:29–30; Eph. 1:4–5)
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul’s critics could point to his absence from Jesus’ earthly ministry and his late arrival among the apostles. His reply is the chronology of vv. 17–22: he went to Arabia rather than Jerusalem, waited three years, stayed a fortnight, met two men, then vanished into Cilicia for years, and the Judean churches would not have recognised him in the street. If his gospel came from that world, its members would at least have known his face.

Now: A disqualifying history made into evidence (vv. 13–14), a calling that began before the one called was looking (v. 15), and hidden years that turn out to be part of the work (vv. 17, 21–22) — three things that reach an ordinary believer directly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s gospel is not human in origin; he received it by revelation of Jesus Christ.

Not man’s gospel. Neither invented nor taught to him by others.

Revelation of Jesus Christ. On the Damascus road and after (Acts 9; 26:16).

What it does not mean. Not that Paul received no information from others (1 Corinthians 15:3), but that his gospel and commission came straight from Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s past proves that only God could have changed him: he was a zealous persecutor and a rising star in Judaism.

Persecuted violently. Tried to destroy the church (Acts 8:3).

Advancing in Judaism. Outstripping his peers.

Traditions of my fathers. The oral law of the Pharisees.

On a Tuesday. No one is too far gone for God to call. Pray for the most hostile person you know.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s conversion and call were entirely God’s doing: chosen before birth, called by grace, shown his Son.

Set apart before I was born. Like Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5) and the Servant (Isaiah 49:1).

Called by his grace. Effectual calling: God’s initiative, not Paul’s search.

To reveal his Son in me. An inward revelation as well as an outward vision.

Among the Gentiles. His calling and conversion were one event.

Not with flesh and blood. He did not consult anyone.

For worship. Thank God that your conversion too was his idea before it was yours.

parallels.desc: the LORD called me from the womb

verseByVerse.quote: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of going to Jerusalem for approval, Paul went to Arabia, then back to Damascus.

Arabia. The Nabatean kingdom, south and east of Damascus. Whether for reflection or preaching (Aretas, its king, later tried to arrest him, 2 Corinthians 11:32) is unknown.
verseByVerse.note: Arabia here is the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three years after his conversion, Paul visited Peter for just two weeks, and saw only James besides.

To visit Cephas. Historēsai, to get to know: probably to hear from Peter about Jesus’ life.

James the Lord’s brother. Counted among the apostles in a broad sense.

Fifteen days. Too short for an apprenticeship.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. James the Lord’s brother led the church in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: (In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul swears before God that his account is true.

Before God. The facts matter, because his opponents had twisted them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul then worked far from Jerusalem, unknown by sight to the churches of Judea.

Syria and Cilicia. Including Tarsus and Antioch (Acts 9:30; 11:25–26).
verseByVerse.note: Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus.

verseByVerse.quote: They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Judean churches heard only that their persecutor was now preaching the faith, and they glorified God because of him.

The faith. Already a name for the Christian message.

They glorified God. The proper response to a transformed life. A converted persecutor is God’s work, not man’s.

For worship. Give glory to God for someone whose life he has changed.

2.title: Justified by Faith: The Gospel Confronts the Church
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the biographical argument’s climax and the letter’s theological turning point. Two episodes dominate: the Jerusalem conference (vv. 1–10), where the apostles affirmed Paul’s gospel of grace without requiring Gentile circumcision; and the Antioch confrontation (vv. 11–14), where Paul opposed Peter to his face because Peter’s behavior contradicted the gospel he believed. Both episodes illustrate the same point: the gospel of justification by faith alone is the non-negotiable centre of Christianity, and it must be defended even when the offender is the most respected leader in the church.

The chapter’s second half (vv. 15–21) is the theological centrepiece of the entire letter — the most concentrated statement of justification by faith in Paul’s letters apart from Romans 3. “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” The verb “justified” (dikaioō) is a forensic term: to be declared righteous by the divine judge, to have one’s legal status before God established as “not guilty.” This declaration is made not on the basis of law-keeping (which can only expose and condemn sin) but on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ.

The chapter ends with the most luminous personal testimony in Paul’s letters: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” This is the gospel arriving at its destination: not merely a changed legal status but a transformed life — union with Christ, the old self crucified, the new life animated by faith in the one who loved and gave himself for me, personally, individually, sacrificially.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Paul Accepted by the Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 opens with a number that is itself the argument: after fourteen years of preaching and planting without Jerusalem laying a hand on his message. He goes up with Barnabas, who had once vouched for him when the Jerusalem church would not go near him, and with Titus, an uncircumcised Greek — not a companion so much as an exhibit. In v. 2 he goes because of a revelation, not by summons, and meets the leaders privately rather than staging a public showdown he could have won.

His stated purpose, to make sure he was not “running in vain,” is easily misread as doubt about his gospel; chapter 1 forbids that. The danger he is guarding against is that the church might become two churches, a circumcised one and an uncircumcised one, each with its own apostle and its own terms.

Verse 3 gives the verdict in one line: even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. With the test case standing in the room, Jerusalem did not require him to become a Jew. Verses 4–5 explain the pressure that made this a fight. The language is the language of espionage — false brothers secretly brought in, men who slipped in to spy out the freedom of the Gentile churches, whose stated object was slavery. Paul did not yield even for a moment, and gives a pastoral reason rather than a principled one: so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you. Doctrinal firmness is a man standing in a doorway so that people behind him can stay free.

Verse 6 reports the outcome in a phrase — they added nothing to me — and grounds it in the fact that God shows no partiality, a principle Paul turns on the apostles themselves. Verses 7–8 set out the shape of the agreement: Paul entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised just as Peter to the circumcised, one gospel and two mission fields, with God himself named as the one who worked through both men. In v. 9 the order of the clauses carries the theology: the pillars first perceived the grace that was given and only then gave the right hand of fellowship — recognition of what God had done, not a handshake that conferred it. And v. 10 adds the single request Jerusalem made, that they remember the poor, which Paul was already eager to do.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Gospel, One People, One Way In

The Titus decision of v. 3 settles a question of the first order: justification is on identical terms for Jew and Gentile, and no covenant marker supplements faith at the point of acceptance with God. This is not a statement about cultural inclusion; it is a claim about the nature of justification itself, and the Reformed understanding of the covenant of grace — one covenant, one people, one Saviour, one way of entry — finds its clearest apostolic expression here.

Two further principles sit inside the passage. The word entrusted (v. 7) is a steward’s word, and it quietly disqualifies everyone in the dispute from editing the message: Paul may not adjust it to suit Gentiles and Jerusalem may not adjust it to suit Jews, for the same reason, which is that neither owns it. And the sequence of v. 9 — grace perceived, then fellowship extended — gives the church its permanent task in recognising anyone. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. The church perceives what God has given and says so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Galatia was being told that Gentile believers needed circumcision added to their faith. Paul’s answer is that he took this precise question to Jerusalem with an uncircumcised Greek at his side (vv. 1–3), and the men whose authority the Judaizers were invoking added nothing (v. 6) and shook his hand (v. 9). The Judaizers are not following the Jerusalem apostles; they are contradicting them.

Now: Anything may be done for the gospel; nothing may be added to it — which is why Paul could later circumcise Timothy (Acts 16:3) and would not let anyone touch Titus. The same test still sorts real questions from false ones. Where a practice is offered as helpful, Christians may differ; where it is required for full acceptance, the gospel is at stake. And v. 10 guards the other flank: having refused to add one item to the gospel, Paul accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur, because that is not an addition but what grace does once it has arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fourteen years later Paul laid his gospel before the Jerusalem leaders, not to seek permission but to secure the unity of the church.

Fourteen years. From his conversion, or from the first visit.

Which visit? Where scholars differ. Some identify this with the council of Acts 15; others with the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:27–30. Verdict: the famine visit fits better: Paul says he went because of a revelation (Agabus’s prophecy), the meeting was private, and he does not mention the council’s decree, which would have settled the Galatian dispute.

Titus. A Gentile believer: a test case.

Running in vain. Not doubting his gospel, but concerned that a split with Jerusalem would wreck the mission.
verseByVerse.note: It is debated whether this visit is the famine visit of Acts 11 or the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15.

verseByVerse.quote: But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery— to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jerusalem apostles did not require Titus, a Greek, to be circumcised, though false brothers pressed for it; Paul refused to yield for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain.

False brothers. Infiltrators posing as believers.

Spy out our freedom. Freedom from the law as a means of acceptance with God (5:1).

Not for a moment. Contrast Timothy, whom Paul circumcised for mission (Acts 16:3): there it was a voluntary concession; here it was demanded as necessary for salvation.

On a Tuesday. Be flexible about customs, immovable about the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek, uncircumcised — a test case for whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),
verseByVerse.commentary:
The respected leaders added nothing to Paul’s gospel; they recognised that God had entrusted him with the Gentiles as he had Peter with the Jews.

Seemed to be influential. Paul respects them but refuses to be overawed: God shows no partiality.

Added nothing. His gospel needed no correction.

The same God worked. One gospel, two mission fields.

verseByVerse.quote: and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James, Peter and John gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, asking only that they remember the poor.

Pillars. Leaders of the Jerusalem church.

The grace given to me. They recognised God’s work.

Remember the poor. Which Paul did, with the great collection (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

On a Tuesday. Unity in the gospel shows itself in care for the poor.
verseByVerse.note: Pillars held up a building; these three were the leaders of the Jerusalem church. The poor were the believers in Judea.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul recounts how he confronted Peter at Antioch. Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers, but when men came from James he drew back and separated himself, afraid of the circumcision party, and other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed his lead in this pretence. Paul saw that they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, so he challenged Peter publicly: if you, a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you force Gentiles to live like Jews?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Governs the Feet, Not Only the Confession

Peter’s failure was not doctrinal. He had proclaimed the equality of Jew and Gentile before God and won the argument for it. What v. 14 exposes is a gap between a confession genuinely held and a life not walking in line with it — which is what hypocrisy means in Paul’s usage, not the cynical pretence of faith one does not have. The Reformers’ principle that the church is always to be reformed by the gospel bites here: the gospel must govern table habits, social pressure and power dynamics, not merely statements of faith.

There is a further point of some weight. Peter is treated in this passage as a fallible man who can be publicly withstood and corrected by another apostle on a matter of the gospel — and Scripture records it without embarrassment. Whatever authority the Jerusalem leadership had, it was never authority over the message, which is precisely the argument of vv. 6–9.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter’s withdrawal at Antioch was socially motivated, not theologically: v. 12 says he feared the circumcision party. It is the same snare Paul named at 1:10 — am I trying to please man? — and it swept up the whole Jewish contingent and Barnabas with it (v. 13).

Now:Two things in this section reach a reader directly: the room in which he is a slightly different Christian, and the question of when a leader should be confronted in public. Paul’s case meets every condition at once — public conduct, the gospel itself at stake, others being carried away, and the rebuke spoken to Peter’s face rather than about him — and the friendship survived it (2 Pet. 3:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Peter withdrew from eating with Gentile believers, Paul opposed him publicly, because his conduct contradicted the gospel.

To his face. Openly, not behind his back.

Ate with the Gentiles. Table fellowship expressed full acceptance (Acts 10:28; 11:3).

Fearing the circumcision party. Peter, who had denied Jesus out of fear, fell again into the fear of people.

Where Christians differ: Peter’s authority. Roman Catholic teaching holds Peter as the first pope. Here an apostle rebukes him publicly for error in practice. Verdict: no church leader is above correction by the gospel; Scripture, not any office, is the final authority.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch in Syria was the first great Gentile church. Eating together was the test: strict Jews would not share a table with Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hypocrisy spreads: the other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed Peter, so Paul confronted him for not walking in line with the truth of the gospel.

Even Barnabas. The encourager, Paul’s partner, who had championed Gentile believers (Acts 11:22–26).

Not in step with the gospel. Behaviour can deny doctrine. Separating from Gentile believers implied they were second-class.

Live like a Gentile. Peter himself had lived freely; now he was pressuring Gentiles to live like Jews.

On a Tuesday. Whom do you avoid at church because of class, race or background? That too contradicts the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas had been Paul’s partner on the first journey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul spells out the principle. Even Jewish believers know that no one is justified by doing what the law requires but only through faith in Jesus Christ, so they too have trusted Christ in order to be justified by faith. If seeking justification in Christ shows that we are still sinners, that does not make Christ a servant of sin; rebuilding the law as a way of standing with God is what makes a person a transgressor. Through the law Paul died to the law so that he might live for God. He has been crucified with Christ; his life now is Christ living in him, and he lives by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him. He will not set aside God’s grace, for if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith: The Article by Which the Church Stands or Falls

Protestant theology came to call justification by faith articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae, the article by which the church stands or falls — a summary of Luther’s own conviction — and vv. 15–21 are the classic passage for it. Justification is forensic — a declaration of status, not an infusion of goodness, though transformation certainly follows. It is by faith alone, its object is Christ alone, and it is by grace alone; and the Reformed tradition has always insisted the three stand or fall together. If faith is not the exclusive instrument, it is not by grace; if Christ is not the exclusive object of faith, it is not grace either.

One point of translation deserves noting since a reader may meet it. The phrase rendered faith in Jesus Christ in v. 16 can also be read as “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ” — his own obedience to the cross as the ground of acceptance. The majority Reformed rendering takes it as faith directed toward him; either way, faith is not a work that earns the verdict but the empty hand that takes it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish believers had every religious advantage and still came the same way as the Gentiles they were now refusing to eat with (v. 15). The argument from the insider to the outsider is conclusive: if the law cannot justify those to whom it was given, it will not justify anyone else. And v. 18 lands directly on Antioch, where stones were going back into a wall that had been pulled down.

Now:The person who comes to faith from a life of moral respectability and the person who comes from obvious wreckage stand on identical ground, with the same righteousness, which is Christ’s. The respectability is as irrelevant to the verdict as the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Jewish believers know that no one is justified by works of the law but only through faith in Jesus Christ.

Justified. Declared righteous by God, the judge: a legal verdict.

Works of the law. Where Christians differ. The “New Perspective on Paul” (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, N. T. Wright) reads this mainly as Jewish boundary markers (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath) that excluded Gentiles. The Reformed reading holds that while those markers are in view, the principle is wider: no law-keeping of any kind can justify (3:10; Romans 3:20; 4:4–5). Verdict: both social and soteriological: the boundary markers are the presenting issue, but Paul’s answer is that justification is by faith, not by any works.

Faith in Jesus Christ. Where scholars differ. The Greek pistis Christou can mean “faith in Christ” or “the faithfulness of Christ”. Verdict: the verse itself says “we have believed in Christ Jesus”, so faith in Christ is in view; Christ’s faithfulness is the ground on which that faith rests.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeking justification in Christ does not make Christ a promoter of sin.

Found to be sinners. Jews who ate with Gentiles were called sinners by the law’s standard.

Certainly not! Paul’s strongest denial (Romans 6:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the law Paul died to the law, so that he might live to God.

Rebuild what I tore down. Returning to the law as the way of acceptance would prove him a transgressor.

Through the law I died to the law. The law condemned him, and in Christ that sentence was carried out (Romans 7:4).

Live to God. Death to the law is not lawlessness but new life for God.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
United to Christ in his death, the believer now lives a new life by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him.

Crucified with Christ. Perfect tense: a past event with lasting effect.

Christ lives in me. Union with Christ: the believer’s life is Christ’s life in him.

By faith. The daily life of the Christian is lived by faith, not only begun by it.

Who loved me and gave himself for me. Luther said the gospel is in the personal pronouns.

For worship. Read the last sentence aloud, putting your own name in place of “me”.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If righteousness could come by the law, Christ died for nothing.

Nullify grace. Adding the law cancels grace.

For no purpose. The cross is either necessary or pointless.

On a Tuesday. Every attempt to earn God’s favour says the cross was unnecessary. Rest in it instead.

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the theological heart of Galatians: a sustained argument from Scripture that the gospel of grace by faith is not a Pauline novelty but the foundation on which all of God’s dealings with Abraham and his descendants have always rested. The law came 430 years after the Abrahamic covenant. It cannot therefore revoke the promise made to Abraham; it operates within a different register, serving a different purpose, pointing toward its own fulfillment and supersession in Christ.

Paul opens with an emotional appeal: the Galatians had experienced the Spirit. They knew it. Signs and wonders had accompanied their conversion. Did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The answer is obvious — and the answer settles the question about the ground of their acceptance with God. The same Spirit-receiving faith that initiated their Christian life is also the ongoing basis of their standing. Maturity in Christ is not a movement from faith toward law; it is a deepening of faith in the one in whom all the law finds its fulfillment.

The chapter’s christological climax is the most audacious claim in the letter: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (v. 13). The cross was not merely a sacrifice; it was a specific legal exchange. Christ took the law’s curse — the curse pronounced on all who fail to keep it perfectly — onto himself, becoming the accused on behalf of the accused, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has finished defending his apostleship and turns on the Galatians themselves, and the first line has no courtesy in it. In v. 1 he calls them un-minded and asks who has bewitched them, when what had been placarded before their eyes was Jesus Christ crucified. Then, instead of an argument, he asks about their own biography. Verse 2 puts the one question he says is sufficient: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? They knew the answer. They were, for the most part, uncircumcised pagans who heard and believed, and God moved in.

Verse 3 exposes the folly precisely: having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Not sin — religion; the whole realm of what a man can do, mark and show. Verse 4 asks whether their suffering was wasted, and then Paul cannot finish the sentence. Verse 5 makes the question present tense: God is still supplying the Spirit and working miracles among them, and the evidence stands in the room while the argument goes on.

The sentence of v. 5 runs on a dash straight into v. 6, so Abraham is not a new topic but the last clause of the question. Genesis 15:6 is quoted: Abraham believed God and it was posted to his account as righteousness. Verse 7 draws the conclusion that overturns the whole Judaizing offer — it is those of faith who are Abraham’s sons. Verse 8 goes further: Scripture pre-gospelled Abraham, so the Gentiles were in view in God’s first sentence to him. And v. 9 sets every believer alongside the patriarch himself: blessed along with Abraham, on the same footing, in one queue.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Is Received by Faith, and the Reception Settles Everything

The appeal of vv. 2 and 5 is not to religious feeling but to a fact of record: the mechanism by which God gives his Spirit. Reformed theology has always held that the Spirit is the agent of union with Christ and that union with Christ is received by faith alone; here Paul argues it backwards from experience. If the Spirit came through the hearing of the gospel and not through law-works, then the law-works were never the channel, and no later addition can make them one.

The force of v. 3 is that the Christian life is not two-stage. There is no beginning by grace followed by an advance by performance. What justifies also sanctifies, and it is the same Spirit received in the same way from first to last. And vv. 6–9 place this outside the new covenant altogether: Abraham was justified by faith in Genesis 15, two chapters and many years before the sign of circumcision was given in Genesis 17. Justification by faith is not a Christian innovation. It is how God has always dealt with sinners.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were not asking the Galatians to abandon Christ. They were offering completion — take the mark, keep the calendar, and become full sons of Abraham like us. From inside, it looked generous and it looked mature. Paul’s answer in vv. 1–5 is to make them look at their own conversion: nothing in their hands, no circumcision, no Sabbath kept, and God gave them his Spirit. Then vv. 6–9 take Abraham, the Judaizers’ own trump card, and turn it over.

Now: Almost no believer decides to be justified by works; the drift of v. 3 is quieter than that. Over a few years the empty hands fill with real and often good things — a devotional habit, a serving rota, a reputation — and the ground of confidence migrates without anyone noticing the day it moved. The test is the one v. 2 implies. Think of your worst week, and ask whether God was as pleased with you that Sunday as on your best. If something flinches, the flinch is the answer, and vv. 6–9 are the cure: one queue, one way in, and Abraham himself is standing in it.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning from the crucified Christ to the law is so irrational that it looks like enchantment.

Foolish. Unthinking, not unintelligent.

Bewitched. As if under the evil eye: a spell that blinds.

Publicly portrayed as crucified. Like a placard: Paul’s preaching made the cross vivid. The perfect tense: Christ remains the crucified one.

On a Tuesday. Keep the cross before your eyes; legalism creeps in when it fades.
verseByVerse.note: “Bewitched” pictures someone under a spell or the evil eye. “Publicly portrayed” uses the word for a public notice posted for all to read.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their own experience answers the question: they received the Spirit by believing what they heard, not by keeping the law.

Received the Spirit. The mark of being a Christian (Romans 8:9).

Hearing with faith. Believing the message.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Christian life continues as it began: by the Spirit through faith, not by human effort.

Begun by the Spirit. Conversion was God’s work.

Perfected by the flesh. Thinking that maturity comes by self-effort or rituals.

Suffered in vain. They had suffered for the gospel; would they throw it away?

What it does not mean. Not that effort is wrong in sanctification (Philippians 2:12–13), but that the power and the basis are God’s grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith— just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives the Spirit and works miracles among those who believe, as Abraham believed and was counted righteous.

Supplies. Present tense: God keeps giving.

Genesis 15:6. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness: before circumcision and centuries before the law.

Counted. Credited, reckoned: imputation (Romans 4:3–5).

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s true children are those who believe, and Scripture foretold that God would justify the nations by faith.

Sons of Abraham. Not by descent but by faith.

Scripture foreseeing. Scripture is personified: God speaks through it.

The gospel beforehand. Genesis 12:3: in you all nations shall be blessed. The gospel was announced to Abraham.

For worship. If you believe, you belong to Abraham’s family. Thank God for including the nations.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having proved his case from Abraham, Paul now proves it from the law, and he does it by letting the law speak. Verse 10 says something nobody expects: it is not those who break the law who are under a curse but those who rely on it — the serious, observant, early-rising ones. The proof is Deuteronomy 27:26, the last of the twelve curses Israel answered with its own Amen. Four words carry it: everyone, all things, abide by, and do them. The law is not a pass mark; it is a seamless garment, and it cannot be scored out of a hundred.

Verse 11 states the conclusion as something already plain — no one is justified before God by the law — and grounds it in Habakkuk 2:4, the verse that broke the medieval church open. Verse 12 sets the opposing principle beside it from Leviticus 18:5: the one who does them shall live by them. A thoughtful reader feels the difficulty, since Leviticus is God’s word too. The answer is that the law’s offer was never a bluff; the fault lies not in the law but in the material it works with.

Then v. 13, the summit of the chapter. Christ redeemed us — bought us out of the slave market — from the law’s curse by becoming a curse himself, and the text quoted is Deuteronomy 21:23, the very verse that made a crucified Messiah unthinkable to Saul the Pharisee. Verse 14 gives the purpose twice: so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith — which closes the circle opened by the question in v. 2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Curse Exchanged

That Christ bore the penalty due to sinners in their place, exhausting the law’s sentence, is not a later development of doctrine but the explicit content of v. 13. The exchange is legally precise. The curse of vv. 10–12 fell on him, so that the blessing of v. 14 could fall on those who have no claim to it. This is not sympathetic solidarity — he suffered with us — but substitution: he suffered instead of us, bearing what was ours.

Two guards belong here. First, becoming a curse does not mean the Father ceased to love the Son or turned on him in temper; Jesus said the opposite (John 10:17). The sentence was real and the Father’s delight in the obedient Son was real at the same hour. Second, the Deuteronomy text is about the public display of an already-condemned man, so the tree did not make him cursed — it published the verdict. Saul had read that publication correctly and been wrong about only one thing: whose curse it was.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the law as a supplement, a way of securing what faith had begun. Verses 10–12 show that the law has no supplementary setting. It accepts one condition only, and no son of Adam has ever met it, so those who take their stand there have entered a system whose only two verdicts are flawless obedience and curse. Verse 13 names the single exit, and vv. 13–14 together explain how a Gentile with no covenant and no ancestry ends up holding the Spirit of God.

Now: Some readers come to v. 10 with their stomach already tight, half expecting confirmation that God is disappointed with them. Read it exactly. The curse is aimed not at their failure but at the thing they were using to cover it. And v. 13 says what became of it: the sentence was carried out, and not on you. Verse 14 adds that the Spirit you already have is the receipt.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Relying on the law brings a curse, because the law requires perfect obedience, which no one gives.

Deuteronomy 27:26. Cursed is everyone who does not keep all of it.

The unstated premise. No one does keep it all (Romans 3:23; James 2:10).

On a Tuesday. If you try to stand before God on your record, you stand under a curse. There is a better way.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture itself shows that righteousness comes by faith, not by the law, which works on a different principle.

Habakkuk 2:4. The righteous shall live by faith: the text that set Luther free.

Leviticus 18:5. The law says: do and live. Its principle is performance.

Two ways. Faith receives; law achieves. They cannot be mixed as the ground of acceptance.

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith
by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ took the law’s curse on himself in our place, hanging on the tree, to redeem us.

Redeemed. Bought us out of slavery.

Becoming a curse for us. Substitution: he bore the curse we deserved (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Deuteronomy 21:23. One hanged on a tree is cursed. The crucifixion, which seemed to disprove Jesus’ messiahship, was actually God’s way of removing the curse.

Where Christians differ: penal substitution. Some modern theologians reject the idea that Christ bore God’s judgment in our place, calling it cosmic child abuse. Scripture presents the Son willingly giving himself (2:20), the Father and Son united in love. Verdict: penal substitution is clearly taught here and is the heart of the atonement.

For worship. The curse that was yours fell on him.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law, the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree was under God’s curse.

parallels.desc: a hanged man is cursed by God

verseByVerse.quote: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ bore the curse so that Abraham’s blessing would reach the Gentiles, and we would receive the promised Spirit through faith.

The blessing of Abraham. Justification and the Spirit.

Through faith. Again and again.

parallels.desc: I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temperature drops and Paul takes the Galatians from Golgotha to a lawyer’s office, calling them brothers again, a warm word breaking through the anger. Verse 15 gives the principle from everyday life: once a covenant or will has been ratified, no one annuls it or adds a clause. If that holds for a document drawn up by men who forget things and change their minds, how much more for one God has sworn. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise; they were proposing an amendment, and an amendment is not a modest adjustment but a legal impossibility.

Verse 16 makes the exegetical observation that troubles modern readers: the promise was made to Abraham’s offspring, singular, who is Christ. Since the word is collective in both Hebrew and Greek, this looks like a trick — until you notice that Paul himself uses it collectively in v. 29. The argument is not about grammar in isolation but about the shape of the history. The promise narrowed at every fork: Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau, Judah, David. It was always funnelling toward one person.

Verse 17 dates it. The law came 430 years after the promise, and the later document cannot cancel the earlier one; the figure follows the Greek Old Testament Paul’s churches used, which counts from Abraham to the exodus. Verse 18 states the either-or underneath: if the inheritance comes by law it no longer comes by promise. These are not two ingredients that improve each other but two answers to the question of who is responsible for my standing, and the second cancels the first.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priority and Indestructibility of the Promise

The covenant of grace — God’s unconditional oath to bless all nations through Abraham’s seed — is prior to the Mosaic law and independent of it. This is a foundation of Reformed covenant theology, and vv. 15 and 17 are where Paul argues it. The Mosaic administration does not replace the Abrahamic covenant or amend its terms; it operates within it and serves it for a season, leaving its character as promise untouched.

Verse 16 supplies the reason the promise cannot fail, and it is more than a point of grammar. Had God covenanted with Abraham’s descendants as a body, the covenant would have rested in the hands of a nation that broke every arrangement it was given. He covenanted with one heir who would not break it, and everyone else inherits by being in him. Verse 18 draws the practical edge: God “has given” it, in the perfect tense, and it stands given. A promise whose security is the character of the one who swore it is a different kind of possession from anything conditioned on the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were arguing, in effect, that the later Mosaic legislation modified the conditions of the earlier Abrahamic promise. Verses 15 and 17 show why that is not a theological preference but a legal impossibility, and v. 18 shows what it would cost if it were allowed: not an improved promise but no promise at all. Verse 16 removes their last foothold by identifying the heir they were claiming to represent.

Now: The difference v. 18 describes is invisible from the outside. Two Christians can keep the same hours, give the same money and serve on the same rota, one obeying a Father who has already given him the house, the other trying to secure a house he is not sure of. You can tell them apart only when something goes wrong: one fails and runs to his Father, the other fails and hides, because for him the failure has moved the inheritance. Verses 15–18 exist to put every reader in the first category and keep him there.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even a human covenant cannot be changed once ratified, and God’s promises were made to Abraham and to his one offspring, Christ.

A human example. A ratified will cannot be altered.

Offspring, singular. “Seed” is a collective noun, but Paul sees that the promise culminates in one person, Christ, and includes all who are in him (v. 29).
verseByVerse.note: “Offspring” (literally “seed”) is a singular noun that can refer to one descendant or many.

parallels.desc: in your offspring shall all the nations be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law came 430 years after the promise and cannot cancel it: the inheritance depends on promise, not law.

430 years. Exodus 12:40, from the patriarchs to Sinai.

By promise. Grace, not wages.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt; Paul uses the figure for the long gap between the promise and the law.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify, cannot give life and cannot amend the promise, the obvious objection has to be faced, and v. 19 faces it: why then the law? Paul answers with three phrases, each of which puts the law in its place without insulting it. It was added because of transgressions — drawing the line that turns vague wrongness into named counts. It was until the offspring should come, with an expiry written into it, not a failure but a term. And it was put in place through angels by an intermediary, which is the sharpest demotion of all.

Verse 20 is the most compressed sentence in the letter, and honest commentators admit that its details are disputed. But the direction is clear from the chain Paul has just counted. A mediator implies two parties; the presence of Moses on the mountain tells you Sinai was a two-sided arrangement that could fail, and it failed at the foot of the mountain. God is one: when he came to Abraham there was no second party, and in Genesis 15 he passed alone between the pieces while Abraham slept through his own covenant.

Verse 21 asks whether the law is therefore contrary to God’s promises and answers with Paul’s strongest negative. They are not rivals but a diagnosis and a cure. He grants freely that if any law could give life, righteousness would have come that way. Verse 22 gives the true verdict: Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, shut in like fish in a net, so that the promise might be given by faith. Verses 23–25 name the jailer’s office — the law was our paidagōgos, the household slave who walked the boy to school until he came of age. Verse 24 says he was doing it so we might be justified by faith, and v. 25 says the arrangement has ended.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Genuine, Severe, Temporary, Fulfilled

Reformed theology has always held to the unity of the covenant of grace across both Testaments while recognising the distinct function of the Mosaic administration within it. Verses 19 and 24 are the classic ground for that. The law was genuinely from God, genuinely binding in its time, and genuinely serving the covenant of grace — but it was designed for a phase and not for the end. Its close as a system of justification is not God changing his mind; it is God completing his plan.

Two guards belong with vv. 23–25. It does not follow that God’s moral will has been repealed: Paul will say in 5:14 that the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour. What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the guardianship under which the people of God lived as minors. Nor does it follow that Old Testament believers were second-class. They were children in the same family under the care their age required. And v. 22 shows the severity was mercy: the exits were closed so that the one open door would finally be taken.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted the guardian reinstated after the child had come of age. Verse 19 answers that the guardian was appointed for a term that has expired, v. 20 that the promise never depended on two signatures anyway, and v. 25 that the arrangement is over.

Now: Verses 21–25 meet three readers: the one who assumes his problem is information or willpower, the one who finds that the harder he tries the worse the accounting gets, and the largest group of all — believers who are adults in Christ and still live as if under supervision.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law was added for a time, because of transgressions, until Christ came.

Because of transgressions. To expose sin, define it, restrain it and even increase awareness of it (Romans 5:20; 7:7).

Until the offspring. The law as a covenant administration was temporary.

Through angels. Jewish tradition held angels were present at Sinai (Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2).

Where Christians differ: the law today. Some say the law has no role for Christians. Reformed theology distinguishes three uses: to convict of sin, to restrain evil in society, and to guide believers in grateful obedience (the “third use”). Verdict: the Mosaic covenant has ended, but the moral law remains God’s good guide for his people (Romans 13:8–10).
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law; Moses was the intermediary.

parallels.desc: I stood between the LORD and you

verseByVerse.quote: Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law came through a mediator between two parties; the promise came directly from the one God.

A famously obscure verse. Some count hundreds of interpretations. The likeliest: the law was a two-sided arrangement mediated by Moses, while the promise was God’s unilateral commitment.

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law does not contradict God’s promises; it was never able to give life, and it locked everyone under sin so that the promise might be given to those who believe.

Certainly not! The law is good (Romans 7:12).

Could not give life. The law shows the way but cannot give power to walk it.

Imprisoned under sin. Scripture shuts every mouth (Romans 3:19), so that the only way out is faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law was a temporary guardian until Christ came; now that faith has come, we are no longer under it.

Held captive. In protective custody.

Guardian. Paidagōgos, the slave who supervised a child until adulthood: a strict minder, not a teacher.

Until Christ came. A turning point in history, and in each believer’s life.
verseByVerse.note: The “guardian” (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised a child, took him to school and kept him in line until he came of age.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Through faith, all of them are sons of God in Christ Jesus, for all who were baptised into Christ have put him on like a garment. In him the divisions that ruled the ancient world, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, no longer determine anyone’s standing; all are one in Christ. And if they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s offspring and heirs of the promise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ, and the Unity It Creates

Verses 26–27 give the ground of everything Paul has argued: the believer’s standing is not a quality in himself but a location. He is in Christ, clothed in Christ, and therefore holds the status of the Son. This is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well; the clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer.

Verse 28 is the theological ground of the New Testament’s social revolution. The gospel does not merely change individuals, it creates a community in which the stratifications of the old age no longer determine worth or access. Sincere believers who honour this book read the verse differently when it comes to office and order, some hearing the end of every distinction of role, others holding that Paul speaks of standing here and of roles elsewhere, which is the more natural reading of the whole Pauline corpus. What neither side qualifies is what the verse indisputably says, and it is the larger thing: at the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance of v. 29 there is no smaller share.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jew and Greek was a divide so absolute that a Jew would not enter a Gentile house; slave and free described perhaps a third of a city’s population as property; male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. A saying recorded in later rabbinic sources thanked God for not having been made a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Verse 28 takes those three walls and says they do not run through the room. Verses 26–27 explain why: everyone in it is wearing the same garment. Verse 29 tells Gentile believers they are not associate members of a Jewish covenant but full heirs.

Now:Every congregation holds people who have quietly concluded they are second rank. Verse 28 does not offer them a role; it says something better and harder to believe, that Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building.

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through faith in Christ, all believers are God’s sons, clothed with Christ in baptism.

Sons. Full heirs, not children under a guardian.

Put on Christ. Like a new garment (Romans 13:14).

Baptised into Christ. Where Christians differ. Sacramental traditions see baptism as the means of union with Christ; Baptists see it as the sign of a union already received by faith. Verdict: faith unites us to Christ (v. 26), and baptism publicly signifies and seals that union; the two are closely linked in the New Testament, which knows nothing of unbaptised believers.

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ, no ethnic, social or sexual distinction gives anyone a better standing before God: all are one.

Neither Jew nor Greek. Echoing a Jewish morning prayer that thanked God for not being made a Gentile, a slave or a woman.

Where Christians differ. Egalitarians use this verse to argue against any distinction of roles for men and women in church and home. Complementarians answer that the verse concerns standing before God and inheritance in Christ (v. 29), not the abolition of every distinction, which Paul upholds elsewhere (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Timothy 2:12). Verdict: the app’s complementarian view: equal in worth and inheritance, distinct in some roles.

On a Tuesday. No one in your church is a lesser Christian because of race, class or sex.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Belonging to Christ makes believers Abraham’s offspring and heirs of the promise.

Christ’s. The one offspring (v. 16) includes all who belong to him.

For worship. Thank God that his promise to Abraham is now yours.
