4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the emotional and theological apex of the letter’s central argument. Paul has shown that the law functions as a guardian for children; now he shows what the alternative is: full sonship, the Spirit of the Son, and the cry of “Abba! Father!” from the depths of the adopted heart. The contrast is not merely between two systems but between two existences — the existence of the slave who must perform, and the existence of the son who simply belongs.

The chapter’s opening argument (vv. 1–7) draws on the legal reality of an heir who is underage: he possesses everything but controls nothing, lives under guardians and managers until the time set by the father. Israel under the law was in this condition — heirs of the promise but living under the law’s custody until “the fullness of time.” Then God acted: he sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And confirmation: he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who cries “Abba! Father!” — the most intimate address to God in all of Scripture, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), now placed on the lips of every adopted child of God.

The chapter then turns to a personal appeal (vv. 12–20) of remarkable emotional intensity — Paul reminding the Galatians of how they received him when he first came to them, sick and in need, and how they would have plucked out their eyes for him. His anguish over their drift is the anguish of a parent whose children are being led away: “for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you!” Finally, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah (vv. 21–31) makes the theological point in narrative form: the two covenants produce two kinds of children, and only the children of the free woman — the children of promise, of grace, of the Spirit — are the true heirs of the heavenly Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul illustrates with an heir who is still a child: though he owns the estate, he is no better off than a slave, living under guardians until the time his father has set. In the same way, we were enslaved to the basic principles of this world. But when the appointed time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman and born under the law, to redeem those under the law so that we might be adopted as sons. And because they are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying out “Abba! Father!” So they are no longer slaves but sons, and heirs through God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption, and the Double Sending of Son and Spirit

Verses 4–6 are among the most trinitarian sentences Paul ever wrote. The Father sends the Son; the Father sends the Spirit of the Son. The two missions are distinct and inseparable: the Son accomplishes redemption and adoption as objective legal realities outside us, and the Spirit applies them within, so that the adopted child knows the Father and calls him by name.

Adoption (huiothesia) is the doctrine this chapter states most clearly, and it goes beyond forgiveness. In Roman practice the adopted son took the father’s name, inherited on the same footing as any natural son, and, in some forms of Roman adoption, found his former obligations extinguished; the act was witnessed and irreversible, because what had changed was not his conduct but his family. Verse 7 draws the conclusion in three words — no longer, son, heir — and adds through God, so that nobody imagines an inheritance of this size arriving any other way. J. I. Packer called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians already had everything vv. 4–7 describe. They had the Spirit, they had cried Abba, they were heirs. The Judaizers were offering them a route to a standing they already held, and Paul’s answer in vv. 1–3 is to show them what they would be going back to: the nursery, the guardians, the managers, and a calendar. A son does not earn his way into a family he is already in.

Now:The test v. 3 suggests catches good practices rather than bad ones, and v. 6 answers the reader who does not feel like a son: the Spirit is sent because you are one, so the feeling is the consequence of the status and never the cause of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An heir who is still a child lives like a slave under guardians until the date set by his father.

The picture. In Roman law a young heir owned everything in principle, but controlled nothing until the appointed age.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Christ, Jew and Gentile alike were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.

Elementary principles. Stoicheia: the basic elements, possibly the spiritual powers behind religion, or the rudimentary rules of religion itself, Jewish law and pagan ritual alike (v. 9; Colossians 2:8, 20).

We also. Paul puts the law and paganism on the same side as forms of bondage before Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The “elementary principles” may mean the basic rules of religion, or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the right moment in history God sent his own Son, fully human and under the law, to redeem those under the law and make us his adopted children.

The fullness of time. God’s appointed moment: Roman roads and peace, Greek language, Jewish expectation.

Sent forth his Son. The Son existed before he was sent.

Born of woman. Truly human. Born under the law: a Jew obliged to keep it, and he kept it perfectly.

To redeem. By bearing the law’s curse (3:13).

Adoption. Full rights as sons and heirs.

For worship. Christmas in a sentence. Thank the Father for sending his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because believers are God’s sons, he has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying “Abba! Father!”

The Spirit of his Son. The Trinity in the gospel: the Father sends the Son and the Spirit.

Abba. Jesus’ own Aramaic word for his Father (Mark 14:36), now on our lips. Intimate, though not childish.

No longer a slave. And if a son, then an heir through God.

On a Tuesday. When you pray today, begin with “Father”, and mean it.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before they knew God, the Galatians were enslaved to beings that are not really gods. Now that they know God, or rather are known by him, how can they turn back to those weak and worthless principles and want to be enslaved again, observing special days and seasons? Paul fears his labour among them was wasted. He pleads with them to become like him, as he became like them. He recalls how they welcomed him when he first preached to them because of a bodily illness, treating him like an angel of God, even like Christ, and would have torn out their eyes for him. Has he become their enemy by telling the truth? The rivals court them for selfish ends. Paul, like a mother in labour again until Christ is formed in them, wishes he could be with them, because he is at a loss about them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Symmetry of Bondage, and the Goal of Ministry

Paul’s equation in vv. 8–10 of Judaizing observance with the pagan calendar the Galatians had left is about function, not moral equivalence: any God-given thing made the ground of acceptance will behave like an idol. Reformed theology has always held that moralism is not a minor error but a rival gospel that produces its own bondage.

Verse 9 also contains one of Paul’s clearest incidental statements of election, dropped in as a pastoral correction rather than a seminar topic. To be known by God is not for God to learn facts but for God to set his love on a person and claim him (Jer. 1:5). And v. 19 supplies the only metric for ministry the New Testament finally accepts: not attendance, giving or doctrinal precision, but Christ formed — morphōthē, taking shape from within, the word used of a child forming in the womb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had loved Paul extravagantly in vv. 14–15 and had cooled by v. 16, and vv. 17–18 explain the mechanism. The Judaizers courted them, flattered them, and held the door a few inches short of open. Verse 20 shows what Paul wanted instead: not their allegiance to him but Christ formed in them, which is why he would rather have been in the room than winning on paper.

Now:Verse 10 raises the question every honest reader asks about Christmas, Easter and Sunday, and Paul answers it himself in Romans 14:5–6: what he attacks here is not the observance but the ground. Verses 17–18 describe spiritual manipulation with uncomfortable accuracy, and v. 13 belongs to the reader whose life has been rerouted by his body.

verseByVerse.quote: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?
verseByVerse.commentary:
To go back to religious rules after knowing God is to return to slavery.

Not gods. Idols.

Known by God. Paul corrects himself: the greater truth is that God knows us.

Turn back. Taking up the law as a means of standing is, for Gentile believers, like going back to paganism.

parallels.desc: no gods, but the work of men’s hands

verseByVerse.quote: You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treating special days and seasons as a means of acceptance with God undoes the work of the gospel.

Days, months, seasons, years. Sabbaths, new moons, festivals, sabbatical years.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Some Christians keep a strict Saturday or Sunday Sabbath as binding law; others see all days as alike. Verdict: the app’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10); the Lord’s Day is a glad privilege for worship and rest, never a condition of acceptance.

Laboured in vain. Paul fears his work among them is lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul appeals personally: he became like a Gentile for them; now they should become like him, free from the law.

Become as I am. Free in Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21).

You did me no wrong. Their past kindness to him.

verseByVerse.quote: You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Paul first came, weak and ill, they welcomed him as if he were an angel, even as Christ himself.

A bodily ailment. Perhaps malaria on the coast, or an eye problem (v. 15; 6:11). Paul’s weakness became the occasion for the gospel to reach them.

As Christ Jesus. They received the messenger as the one who sent him.

On a Tuesday. God can use your weakness, illness or interruption to bring the gospel to someone.
verseByVerse.note: We do not know what the illness was; some think it affected his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their earlier joy in the gospel has gone, and they now treat as an enemy the friend who told them the truth.

Your blessedness. Their happiness when they first believed.

Gouged out your eyes. Perhaps a hint of Paul’s eye trouble; certainly a picture of devotion.

Your enemy? Truth-tellers are often resented.

verseByVerse.quote: They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false teachers court the Galatians for their own ends, to make them dependent on themselves.

Make much of you. Flattery with a motive.

Shut you out. Exclude them from Paul and from full fellowship, so that they will seek the teachers’ approval.

On a Tuesday. Beware of leaders whose attention makes you dependent on them rather than on Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul agonises like a mother in labour until Christ is formed in them.

Little children. Tender, parental.

Again. As if giving birth a second time.

Until Christ is formed in you. The goal of ministry: Christlikeness, not law-keeping.

Perplexed. Paul admits he does not know what to do with them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — Hagar and Sarah: Two Covenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the story of Abraham’s two sons, one by the slave woman Hagar, born in the ordinary way, and one by the free woman Sarah, born by promise. He reads them as two covenants: Hagar stands for Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem, in slavery with her children; Sarah stands for the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother, as Isaiah promised the barren woman many children. Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise. As the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit then, so it is now. Scripture says to drive out the slave woman and her son, so believers are children not of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.theology:
Typology, and Why the Two Covenants Cannot Share a House

Verse 24 is not allegory in the Alexandrian sense that dissolves history. Paul’s premise is that it is written that Abraham had two sons; he treats the mothers, the statuses and the manner of each birth as facts. He is saying the history happened and was designed to carry a meaning the coming of Christ has made visible — which is what the risen Christ himself did on the Emmaus road (Lk. 24:27). If God governs history, a pattern in a true story is not imposed by the reader; it is put there by the author.

Verses 24–25 supply the test that governs the whole section: what a covenant produces tells you what kind of covenant it is. Sinai was genuinely from God and still bore children for slavery, because that was its office. And v. 30 states the reason a mixture is impossible. Add merit to grace and the result is not a moderate position but merit, since the moment performance is part of the ground the whole weight has moved onto it. Two guards belong with v. 30: Paul casts out a system, not persons — he is in labour pains for the people who hold it — and Genesis itself has God hearing Ishmael in the desert and being with him as he grew (Gen. 21:17–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers presented themselves as the true heirs of Abraham. Verse 22 shows that blood was never the mechanism, v. 23 that the difference lay in how each son came to exist, and vv. 24–25 place the Jerusalem establishment on the slave woman’s side. Verse 29 then explains why religious men were persecuting a Gentile church: a man who has spent his life earning his standing cannot hear that a farmer who believed last month is equally accepted, because it writes off the investment. The elder brother of Luke 15:29–30 says nothing untrue about himself and is furious.

Now:Verse 23 finds most readers before the Judaizers do: the situation you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long is Hagar’s tent. And v. 29 is a warning before it is a comfort: watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without having earned it.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law itself, read properly, tells the story of two sons: one of a slave, one of a free woman, one by nature and one by promise.

Do you not listen to the law? Here “law” means the books of Moses.

Ishmael and Isaac. Genesis 16; 21.

By promise. Isaac was born through God’s miracle, not human scheming.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham’s son by the slave woman Hagar was Ishmael; his son by the free woman Sarah was Isaac, born by promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two women represent two covenants: Hagar, Sinai and slavery; Sarah, the promise and freedom.

Allegorically. Paul is not denying the history but drawing out a typological pattern already present in it.

Where Christians differ: allegory. Medieval interpreters often found four senses in every text. The Reformers insisted on the plain historical sense, while recognising typology rooted in the text, as here. Verdict: follow Paul’s inspired typology, but do not invent allegories where Scripture does not.

Present Jerusalem. Paul’s opponents claimed Jerusalem’s authority; Paul says the earthly city, rejecting Christ, is in slavery.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers belong to the heavenly Jerusalem, a free mother who, once barren, now has more children than she can count.

The Jerusalem above. The true city of God (Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2).

Isaiah 54:1. The barren woman rejoices: Zion after exile, fulfilled in the worldwide church.

For worship. You belong to a free city, with a mother who has children from every nation.

parallels.desc: sing, O barren one, who did not bear

verseByVerse.quote: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are children of promise like Isaac, and like him they will be persecuted by those born of the flesh.

Persecuted. Ishmael mocked Isaac (Genesis 21:9). The agitators pressure the Galatians as Paul’s opponents persecuted him.

verseByVerse.quote: But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture says the slave woman and her son must be sent away: grace and law cannot share the inheritance.

Cast out. Sarah’s words, confirmed by God (Genesis 21:10–12). The Galatians must expel the false teaching, not admit it.

Not of the slave but of the free. Believers’ identity is freedom.

On a Tuesday. Live as a free child of God today, not as a slave trying to earn your place.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman with her son

5.title: For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free: The Spirit and the Flesh
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the hinge on which the entire letter turns from theology to life. The freedom Paul has argued for throughout — freedom from the law as a system of justification, freedom from the curse, freedom from the elementary principles of the old age — must now be shown to produce not moral chaos but something far better than law-keeping ever could. The chapter answers two questions that the letter’s argument raises: What does this freedom look like in practice? And what is its alternative to the law as the shaping force of Christian behavior?

The answer to the first question is given negatively and positively. Negatively: freedom is not license (“do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh”). The Judaizers’ accusation — that a gospel without law-requirements would produce moral anarchy — is not left unanswered. But the answer is not to reinstate the law; the answer is to walk in the Spirit. Positively: the whole law is fulfilled in one word — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (v. 14). Those who walk by the Spirit do not need the law to produce love, because the Spirit is the Spirit of the God who is love, and his fruit in the believer is love. The Judaizers’ program produced biting and devouring; the Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

The heart of the chapter is the contrast between the works of the flesh (vv. 19–21) and the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 22–23). The language itself is instructive: works (plural, produced by human striving) versus fruit (singular, the organic product of the Spirit’s life within). The flesh produces a catalogue of self-serving, community-destroying behaviors; the Spirit produces a coherent, integrated character that is nothing less than the character of Christ. The goal of the Christian life is not the avoidance of the flesh’s works by rule-keeping but the cultivation of the Spirit’s life by staying close to the one who gives it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 compresses four chapters into a line: for freedom Christ has set us free. The apparent tautology is the point — freedom is the destination, not a stage on the way to a stricter religion. Stand firm is a military verb, because freedom is not a resting state; slavery is restful in a way liberty is not, since a slave always knows where he stands. The yoke of slavery is Peter’s own phrase for the law at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:10), and it sits against the yoke Jesus offers in Matthew 11:29–30. Nobody goes without a yoke; the question is whose.

Verses 2–3 are the warning. If a man accepts circumcision as what completes his standing, Christ is of no advantage to him — not less, none, because he has changed systems into one that has no column for what somebody else has done. Verse 3 closes the escape route: he is obligated to keep the whole law, not the one item he was sold. Verse 4 states the result in two phrases that describe a change of position rather than of behaviour: severed from Christ, fallen out of the sphere of grace. Verse 5 draws the line with an emphatic we ourselves, and adds the note of waiting; v. 6 says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts, but faith working through love.

Then the appeal. Verse 7 uses a technical word for cutting in on a runner — somebody stepped into their lane. Verse 8 says quietly that this persuasion is not from him who calls them. Verse 9 warns that a little leaven changes the whole loaf, invisibly, while it is happening. Verse 10 is the surprise: Paul is confident about them, in the Lord, and leaves the troubler to God. Verse 11 shows what was being said about him and names the offence of the cross, and v. 12 aims a deliberately shocking wish at teachers who make the knife the mechanism.
verseByVerse.theology:
Freedom as the Goal of Redemption, and What Falling from Grace Means

The Reformed tradition has always held that gospel freedom is more than freedom from sin’s penalty; it is freedom from performance-based religion — liberty to live as sons rather than as slaves calculating wages. This is not antinomianism. The law’s moral demands are fulfilled from within by those who walk in the Spirit rather than imposed from without on those who must earn a standing. Luther’s paradox holds both: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.

Verse 4 must be read for what it says. Both its clauses describe position, not conduct: the people addressed have become more religious, not less, and Paul identifies them in the same breath as those who would be justified by the law. To fall from grace here is to step off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, where Christ’s work is inoperative — not to have disgraced oneself, which is the phrase’s modern and quite different meaning. That Paul writes v. 10 six sentences later, expressing confidence about the very same people, settles how v. 4 is functioning: it is the warning that prevents the thing it describes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Circumcision was offered to the Galatians as an upgrade — a fuller belonging. Verses 2–3 show it is not an upgrade but an exchange, and v. 3 reads them the rest of the contract nobody mentioned. Verse 11 reveals that Paul was being quoted against himself, perhaps on the strength of his past; his answer is his scars. Verse 12 would have landed with local force, since the mother goddess, whose chief shrine was at Pessinus, was served by priests who castrated themselves.

Now:Standing firm (v. 1) usually means refusing to answer “where do I stand with God today?” by reaching for the last few days. Verse 4 describes a man at peace with being justified by his own record, which is the opposite of the reader it frightens; and v. 8 gives a usable test for any new teaching — does it come to you the way the God who called you came to you?

verseByVerse.quote: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.” Christ freed believers so that they would be free — not to move them under a new system of earning God’s favour. They must hold that ground.

Freedom is the destination. “For freedom… free” looks like a stammer. Paul is answering: what is the freedom for? Not for anything beyond itself — not a stage on the way to a stricter, “more mature” religion, nor a probation to prove you deserve something better. Christ didn’t release his people to transfer them to a superior master; he wanted them free. Many Christians treat grace as the doorway and law as the corridor beyond: saved by grace, they then describe a daily life where everything depends on their performance. Paul says door and corridor are made of the same thing.

Stand firm. A military word: hold the position. Freedom is not a resting state. Left alone, a free man drifts back toward slavery, because slavery is restful in a way liberty isn’t. A slave is told what to do and knows where he stands. Freedom asks you to live without a scoreboard, and many find that harder than obedience.

Whose yoke? A yoke was a wooden beam across an animal’s shoulders. Peter used the picture of the law at the Jerusalem council: “a yoke… that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear” (Acts 15:10). And Jesus offers a yoke: “Take my yoke upon you… For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30). The question is never whether you will wear a yoke, but whose.

“Do not submit again.” Literally, don’t let yourselves be subjected. Nobody would force the Galatians; they would agree, for reasons that felt like devotion. And “again”: these Gentiles had never been under Moses. A return to law-keeping would put them back where their paganism had them — performing, appeasing, never sure.

Standing firm on a Wednesday. It mostly means refusing to answer one question the way your instincts want. The question is “where do I stand with God today?” and the instinctive answer reaches for the last few days — how you prayed, how you spoke to your wife, whether you did the thing you swore to stop. Standing firm is declining to answer that way. The week matters a great deal, but it is not the ground you stand on. The day you let it become the ground, the yoke is back on, and nobody had to put it there (John 8:36). Answer the question today with Christ.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke was the wooden frame joining working animals — a picture of burdensome obligation.

verseByVerse.quote: Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul warns: if the Galatians accept circumcision as necessary for salvation, Christ will be of no benefit to them. Anyone who does so obligates himself to keep the whole law. You cannot add one condition to grace; you have switched to a different system entirely.

Paul signs the warning. “Look: I, Paul, say to you.” He sets the full weight of the apostleship he defended in chapters 1–2 on what comes next.

No advantage at all. Not less advantage — none. Startling, because circumcision is small in itself: commanded by God, counting for nothing either way (v. 6), and arranged by Paul for Timothy (Acts 16:3). So the act isn’t the issue; the issue is what it is asked to do. Accepted as what completes your standing with God, it doesn’t add security to Christ. It changes systems. And in that system Christ is no asset, because it doesn’t deal in gifts but in obligations, with no column for what Someone else has done.

Inconsistent? Paul circumcised Timothy and refused for Titus (2:3). The cases are opposite in everything that matters. Titus was a test case: in Jerusalem, as a condition, to prove a Gentile couldn’t be fully accepted otherwise. Paul refused, because the gospel was on the table. Timothy’s mother was Jewish, so every synagogue saw him as an uncircumcised Jew, which would shut every door Paul wanted to preach through. Nobody claimed it justified him; it was access, not standing. Paul’s question each time: is anyone claiming this is necessary? When not, he is flexible to the point of inconvenience. When someone says “you must,” he won’t move an inch. That principle reaches far beyond circumcision: many secondary practices may rightly be taken up in one setting and refused in another, consistently.

May Christians circumcise their sons today, for health or family reasons? Yes. “Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything” (v. 6). Paul himself had Timothy circumcised for the sake of his witness among Jews (Acts 16:3). What is forbidden is circumcision as a requirement for being accepted by God. A Jewish Christian parent may circumcise his son as a mark of his heritage; no one may make it a condition of salvation.

The whole contract. “Every man who accepts circumcision… is obligated to keep the whole law.” The troublers were selling one item. Paul says there is no such thing. The law is a single garment; take hold of a corner and you have taken all of it — every clause, festival, sacrifice, for life, without a single failure (James 2:10). Nobody mentioned that in the sales pitch. Paul reads them the whole contract.

A test. Is anything in your Christian life — a practice, a tradition, a badge — that you treat as necessary for God to accept you? Keep it freely if it is good, but refuse to let it be a condition. If someone tells you “you must” to be right with God, answer with Christ alone.

verseByVerse.quote: You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who seek to be justified by keeping the law have cut themselves off from Christ and “fallen away from grace.” This is not about a moral scandal; it is about leaving the ground of grace to stand on one’s own performance, where Christ does nothing for us.

A frightening verse. The reader most likely to hold it is not a Judaizer but a Christian who has had a bad year or decade and has just read “fallen away from grace” and gone cold. So start with what it says.

Not “fallen from grace” in the popular sense. In everyday speech, “fallen from grace” means disgraced — a scandal or moral collapse. Paul means nothing of the kind. These people hadn’t fallen into sin; they had become more religious, keeping a calendar and considering a rite to please God more thoroughly. Both halves of the sentence describe a change of position, not behaviour. “Severed from Christ” — rendered inoperative, cut off from benefit — applies to “you who would be justified by the law.” And “fallen away from grace” is falling out of grace as out of a place: stepping off the ground of grace, where Christ does his work, onto the ground of law.

The lifeboat. Picture a man in a lifeboat who decides to swim alongside, still holding the rope. He hasn’t stopped believing in the boat; he has stopped being in it, and the boat does nothing for him out there. Law-standing doesn’t add to Christ’s work; it replaces it. No one is partly justified by each.

Verse 10. Six sentences later, to the same people: “I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view.” The man who wrote v. 4 is confident about them. So v. 4 isn’t a verdict on the Galatians; it is the warning that keeps them from what it describes.

For the frightened reader. What does the verse describe? A person seeking to be justified by his own law-keeping and at peace with that. Is that you? If you are afraid because you know your record won’t carry you, that fear is the opposite of Paul’s condition. Nobody standing on his own performance is troubled by the news that performance won’t do. A warning about a cliff is not a report that you have gone over, and those who read it most anxiously are almost always furthest from the edge.

Can a true believer, then, fall from grace and be lost? Arminian Christians read the verse that way: the Galatians were real believers, and by trusting in the law they could forfeit their salvation. The warning is real and must not be blunted. But the more likely reading is that it describes what happens to anyone who seeks to be justified by the law: he has left the only ground on which grace stands. Those whom God has truly justified, he will glorify (Rom 8:30), and warnings like this are the means he uses to keep them. That is why Paul can write verse 4 and verse 10 in the same breath.

What to do today. A change of footing — not more effort but less. Stop asking whether you have done enough to be received; look at what was done for you, and stand there (Romans 11:6; Philippians 3:9). That is all grace has ever asked of anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the Spirit, through faith, believers eagerly wait for the full hope of righteousness. In Christ, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything — only “faith working through love.” Faith that is real shows itself in love.

“We ourselves.” After “you” who seek justification by law, Paul says an emphatic “we” — drawing a line down the room, showing the Galatians which side he stands on and inviting them back across.

Waiting. “Eagerly wait” means waiting for something certainly coming and not yet here. Strange of righteousness, when Paul insists believers are justified already. Both are true, and holding them is the balance of the Christian life. The verdict is passed: righteous in Christ now, with nothing outstanding. What isn’t yet delivered is the state that matches it — the day you are actually like him, when the man you want to be and the man you are become the same man (Romans 8:23–25). Every believer lives in that gap. It is uncomfortable and it isn’t a sign that something has gone wrong.

Why legalists can’t wait. Waiting requires that the outcome be secure without your involvement. A man whose standing depends on his progress can’t afford to wait; he must be visibly getting somewhere or the structure wobbles. The gospel produces patient people because it has already settled the question they would otherwise spend their lives answering.

Neither counts. Coming from Paul after four chapters against circumcision, you might expect “uncircumcision is what counts.” He says neither does. Make your uncircumcision a badge and you play the same game with the pieces reversed — taking pride in the tradition you rejected as others take pride in keeping it (1 Corinthians 7:19; 6:15).

Faith working through love. Does love make faith able to justify — faith plus love saves? No. Love doesn’t qualify faith; it is what faith does. The verb is one of energy: faith is the living thing, and love is faith at work. A faith that produces no love doesn’t need supplementing. It is a report of something that was never there (James 2:17–18; 1 Corinthians 13:2).

A test. Not “have I done enough?” nor “do I believe the right things?” in the abstract, but: is the trust I have placed in Christ doing anything? Don’t look first at your religious activity. Look at the person nearest you who is hardest to love. That is where faith shows whether it is alive. Do one concrete thing for that person this week.

verseByVerse.quote: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galatians were running well, but someone cut in and stopped them from obeying the truth. This persuasion did not come from God, who called them. And a little leaven works through the whole batch: one small condition added to the gospel eventually changes it entirely.

A runner cut off. Paul speaks warmly, like a coach watching a runner with good rhythm who was going to finish. “Hindered” pictures someone cutting in on a runner. Not tiredness — somebody stepped in front. Christians who have gone backwards usually blame a lack of stamina, and often it isn’t that. Somebody cut in: a teacher, a book, a friend with strong opinions, a season under a ministry that made the gospel conditional. Ask of any cooled faith not “why did I run out of energy?” but “who got in front of me, and when?” There is often a date.

“Not from him who calls you.” Paul doesn’t say the teaching is unbalanced or that its advocates mean well. He says God is not behind it — and names God as “him who calls you,” present tense, still calling. You know the voice that called you; this isn’t it.

A test you can use. Does a teaching sound like the God who called you? Not “is it strict?” — God is often strict. But does it come to you the way he came to you? He came with a gift to someone with nothing to offer, and the effect was relief. When a teaching arrives and its effect is that you feel measured, watched and slightly behind, you may not be able to refute it. You can still recognise it isn’t the voice that called you.

Leaven. “A little leaven leavens the whole lump” (cf. 1 Corinthians 5:6). A pinch of sourdough goes into a large batch; for hours nothing seems to happen, then the whole mass has changed. Quantity is irrelevant: a gospel with a small condition attached is not mostly the gospel; given time, it is a different loaf. And the change is invisible while it happens. Nobody in a church losing the gospel can feel it going. Sermons stay biblical, meetings continue, the language is unchanged; what alters first is the atmosphere — measurement quietly arriving in a room once full of relief. That is why Paul writes at this volume about what looks like a modest adjustment.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) spreads through the whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is confident in the Lord that the Galatians will come back to the true view, and the troublemaker will bear his judgment. If Paul still preached circumcision, he would not be persecuted — the offence of the cross would be gone. He wishes the agitators would go all the way and castrate themselves.

Confident in the Lord. After calling them foolish, bewitched and severed from Christ, he is confident about them — and the confidence rests “in the Lord,” not in their good sense or his arguments. That is how a Christian holds on to someone who is drifting. You can be confident in the person, which is optimism and collapses on contact with facts. Or you can write them off, which feels like realism. Paul does neither: he tells the worst honestly and then expects God to keep them — the only ground on which anyone has been kept. Pray for the drifting person you know with that confidence.

“Whoever he is.” A particular man, apparently, whose name Paul may not know. Paul doesn’t organise a campaign; he hands him to God’s judgment and leaves him there.

The scars as evidence. “If I… still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?” Someone was claiming Paul himself taught circumcision when it suited him — his past as a Pharisee would serve nicely — so the Galatians were only being asked to do what the apostle really wanted. Paul answers with evidence: look at my life. Nobody stones a man for preaching what everyone already accepts.

The offence of the cross. “Offense” is skandalon, the stone that trips. What offends isn’t the suffering; the world admires martyrs. It is what the cross says about the onlooker: he could be saved no other way, his religion and decency contributed nothing, he had to be rescued like a criminal (1 Corinthians 1:23). Add circumcision or any requirement and the offence drains away at once, because now there is something to do, and a religion you can contribute to is one the world tolerates. A gospel nobody is annoyed by has usually been adjusted.

“Emasculate themselves.” It reads as a crude outburst until you know the region. Across Asia Minor, with its chief shrine at Pessinus, the mother goddess Cybele was served by priests who castrated themselves in ecstatic worship. Paul’s point: you want to cut flesh to be accepted by God? You already know what that religion looks like — it’s on your doorstep. If the knife is the mechanism, why stop where Moses stopped? It is the most cutting sentence he wrote, showing the Galatians where their road ends.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s bitter wish may allude to the priests of the goddess Cybele in that region, who castrated themselves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They were called to freedom, but they must not use it as an excuse for the flesh; instead they should serve one another in love. The whole law is summed up in one command, to love your neighbour as yourself. If they bite and devour one another, they will be destroyed by each other.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

The relation of law and love in Reformed ethics is exact. The law’s moral demands are not abolished for the believer; they are fulfilled, but from a different source and in a different direction. The law compels from outside and leaves the sinner exposed; love, produced by the Spirit, constrains from within and overflows. This is what the older divines meant by the law written on the heart (Jer. 31:33) — not a different law, but the same law internalised by the Spirit of adoption and obeyed as the expression of a heart that loves the God who gave everything, rather than as the price of his favour.

Verse 13 also settles the charge of antinomianism that has followed the doctrine of free grace since the first century. Paul concedes the danger frankly and then refuses the remedy his opponents wanted. That refusal is the test of whether a man has understood the gospel he preaches: it is easy to answer licence with law, and it undoes everything. And v. 15 exposes the mechanism by which a doctrine of performance destroys a congregation — once standing is earned, every other believer becomes a measurement, and the resulting suspicion has a righteous vocabulary to conduct itself in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were living out v. 15 while arguing about how to be holy, which is not an irony but a mechanism. The very community the Judaizers claimed to be perfecting by law-observance was tearing itself apart, and vv. 13–14 name the only thing that binds a church in the way rules never can.

Now:A church that makes the Christian life primarily about observable markers will always produce the same social weather: pride in those who meet the standard, shame in those who do not, comparison, and division. The cure v. 13 offers is not a new rule but service, given concretely to the person you are still disagreeing with.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are called to freedom — but not to use it as an opening for the sinful nature. Instead, through love they are to serve one another, for the whole law is fulfilled in one command: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Freedom from the law as a way to God is freedom for love.

The objection faced. If people are truly free, what stops them doing as they like? Paul doesn’t dodge it: “do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh.” “Opportunity” is a military word for a base of operations. Your liberty can be occupied. The flesh moves into the space grace has cleared, and its reasoning is always theologically impeccable: I’m not under law; God has forgiven this already; grace is greater than my sin. All three sentences are true, and all three have been used to excuse things that wrecked a family.

Not a fence, but love. The obvious remedy is to bring back the law to keep freedom in bounds. Paul refuses. Having demolished law as the ground of standing, he won’t smuggle it back as the ground of behaviour. His answer to the flesh is love: “through love serve one another” — and the verb is “be slaves to one another.” He has torn the yoke off their shoulders, and the first thing he tells them to do with their freedom is put themselves at each other’s disposal. Luther put it exactly: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. No tension: the slavery Paul fought is slavery to a system in order to be accepted; this is bondage to people because you already are.

So does the law still bind the believer? “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (v. 18) means not under it as a covenant of works, a curse or the ground of our standing. It does not mean that God’s moral will has lapsed. The law still describes what love does: “For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments” (1 John 5:3). Love fulfils the law; it does not abolish it. The Spirit-led Christian does not need the law to make him acceptable, but he is glad of it as a description of the life the Spirit is producing.

“Fulfilled.” Not “summarised,” as if love were an abridgement, but filled full, brought to its intended completion. Every commandment describes what love looks like meeting a particular situation. “Do not steal” is love meeting your neighbour’s property; “do not bear false witness” is love meeting his reputation (Romans 13:8–10). A man who truly loves isn’t evading the law; he is doing what it was written to produce, as a man who loves his wife doesn’t need a rule against reading her letters.

A higher standard. A code can be satisfied; you can reach the end of a list. “As yourself” has no end. Nobody has gone to bed having loved his neighbour as much as he instinctively looks after himself. A test: whom will you serve this week, deliberately, with the energy you usually spend on yourself?

parallels.desc: you shall love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the Galatians keep biting and devouring one another, they will be consumed by one another. A church that ties standing with God to performance turns its members into rivals, and everyone loses.

Three animal verbs. Bite: a cornered creature’s snap, wounding but not fatal. Devour: eating, taking part of the other. Consumed: nothing left. A sequence — in a church.

Fighting about holiness. The Galatian congregations were tearing each other apart over how to be holy. That is not an irony but a mechanism, still the commonest way a good church destroys itself. Once standing before God is tied to performance, every other believer becomes a measurement. If he keeps more than I do, he is a threat, and I must find the flaw that explains him. If he keeps less, he reassures me, and I need him to stay there. Neither is love, and both feel like discernment. Add a real doctrinal disagreement and the whole thing gets a righteous vocabulary, so that people defending their own standing believe they are contending for the truth.

No winner. Paul doesn’t say the strong will eat the weak but “consumed by one another” — everyone loses. The party that prevails is left with a smaller, colder, more suspicious congregation than the one it was fighting for.

A test. In a disagreement you are inside now, ask what you want to be true about the other person. If you would be disappointed to find he was right, or that his motives were good, then whatever the merits of your case, you are biting. The verse doesn’t ask whether your position is correct; Paul obviously thought his was.

The cure. It is in the verse before: “through love serve one another.” Paul doesn’t answer biting with a rule against biting. The antidote to devouring a brother is serving him — deliberately, concretely, while you still disagree (James 4:1–2). It is very hard to keep eating a man you are carrying something for. Find one way to serve the person you are at odds with this week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–26 — The Flesh and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to walk by the Spirit, and they will not carry out the desires of the flesh, for the two are opposed and at war within them. Those led by the Spirit are not under the law. The works of the flesh are plain: sexual sin, impurity, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousy, rage, rivalry, divisions, envy, drunkenness and the like, and those who live this way will not inherit God’s kingdom. The Spirit produces a very different harvest: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, against which no law stands. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions. Since they live by the Spirit, they should keep in step with him, and not become conceited, provoking or envying one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification and Vivification, and Why the Fight Is Evidence of Life

Reformed theology has always described the Christian life as two complementary movements: mortification, the putting to death of the flesh, which v. 24 states as something already done to every believer; and vivification, the coming alive to God, which v. 25 calls keeping in step with the Spirit. Neither is self-powered. The mortification is the application to daily life of what happened to the old self in Christ’s death (2:20); the vivification is the fruit of the Spirit’s indwelling. The believer does not produce either. He participates in both by faith.

The tension between v. 17 and v. 24 is resolved by the image itself. Crucifixion was chosen by Rome precisely because it was slow: a man nailed to a beam was mortally wounded, fixed, going nowhere — and still perfectly capable of shouting. That is the flesh in a believer. Its authority is broken and its outcome settled, and it will go on being audible until the body dies. Verse 21 must be read with the same care. Scripture never confuses a man who falls into a ditch with a man who lives in it, and the ache that makes a tender conscience afraid of that verse is itself the evidence the verse is not describing him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians needed to see that law and moral chaos were not the only two options, and vv. 16–18 give the third. Verse 20 would have been the most uncomfortable line in the letter read aloud in those congregations, since the middle of Paul’s list of fleshly works is a description of what was happening in the room. Verse 25 carries a piece of quiet artistry: stoichōmen, keep in step, is built on the same root as the stoicheia that had them in bondage in 4:3 and 4:9. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

Now:Walking by the Spirit (v. 16) is concrete rather than mystical: asking before the difficult conversation rather than after it, going where he speaks often enough to know his voice, and obeying the small prompt you would rather not have noticed. And v. 26 has a test anyone can run: what happens in you when good news is announced about the believer whose life is flourishing most visibly?

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desires of the sinful nature. Flesh and Spirit are at war within the believer. But those led by the Spirit are not under the law. The Christian life is lived not by a code but by depending on God’s Spirit, who produces what the law demanded.

Walk. A present command: go on walking — the ordinary word for daily conduct. Not soar, fight, or achieve. The plainest verb there is.

What walking by the Spirit means. Not a mystical state some believers have and others lack. It is conducting today in dependence on the Spirit rather than yourself, and it has recognisable parts: asking his help before the difficult conversation, not after; going where he speaks — the Scriptures — often enough to know his voice; obeying the small prompt you would rather not have noticed; doing the next right thing in Someone else’s strength. None of it is exotic. It is dependence spread across an ordinary week.

A promise. “You will not gratify the desires of the flesh” — with a strong negative. The desires won’t necessarily stop, but they won’t be carried out. And note the order, the strategy of Christian holiness: not “stop gratifying the flesh and then you’ll walk by the Spirit,” but walk, and the other follows. Sin is displaced more often than defeated by frontal assault, because a man staring at his temptation and gritting his teeth is still looking at it.

The war is a sign of life. “The desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh.” A settled war inside every believer. Young Christians often assume the conflict means something went wrong at their conversion. It is the reverse. Before conversion there was no war; the flesh had the field. Now something in you wants what God wants, and it won’t be quiet (Romans 7:14–25).

A hard clause. “To keep you from doing the things you want to do” — read one way, the flesh frustrates the good you intend; the other, the Spirit blocks the evil you intend. Both are true, and Paul may mean the whole situation: you are no longer a single, simple will that can do as it pleases. That is the price of being rescued, and it lasts as long as this life.

Led, not under law. “Led” is passive. The troublers offered a code to keep; Paul offers a Person to follow. A code, however holy, stands outside you and tells you what to do. The Spirit is inside, and he doesn’t merely require the life; he produces it (Romans 8:4–14). Before your hardest moment today, ask him for help — and then take the next step.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The works of the flesh are obvious: sexual sin, idolatry and sorcery, a long list of relational sins like strife, jealousy, anger and divisions, and drunkenness and orgies. Those who live this way will not inherit God’s kingdom. Paul means a settled way of life, not the sin a believer fights and hates.

“Works.” The same word as “works of the law,” deliberately. Law-keeping and licence look like opposites; Paul files them together, because both are things a man produces from his own resources. Only the products differ.

The groups. Sexual sin first: “sexual immorality” (any sex outside marriage), impurity, and sensuality — indulgence that has stopped caring who sees. Then religion gone wrong: idolatry and sorcery — the second is pharmakeia, potions, spells and drugs used to bend outcomes. Both try to manage the divine: an idol is a god you can locate; a spell is a result you can arrange.

The long middle. Slow down here. Enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy — eight of the fifteen, more than half, and every one a sin of the church meeting rather than the tavern. The Galatians were biting and devouring one another, and Paul puts the sins of the respectable at the centre of the works of the flesh. A congregation horrified by verse 19 often carries verse 20 as its ordinary weather. Then drunkenness, orgies, “and things like these” — a portrait, not a legal schedule, so no one can plead that his version isn’t listed.

Will not inherit. This disturbs tender consciences. A believer reads the list, finds himself in the middle section within the last month, and concludes the door has closed. Read the verb carefully: “those who do such things” describes the settled practice of a life — those who go on doing them, whose lives are marked by them, who have made their peace with them (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). Not the sin you fought and lost this week and hated yourself for. There is a world of difference between falling into a ditch and living in it, and Scripture never confuses them.

A test. What do you do the morning after? Not whether you sinned — you did, as did everyone reading this — but whether the sin still grieves you and whether you take it anywhere. A man in whom the Spirit lives cannot sin comfortably. The ache that makes you afraid of this verse is evidence the verse isn’t about you. Take this week’s sin from the middle of the list to God by name, and if it was against a person, put it right with them.
verseByVerse.note: “Sorcery” translates a word that also covered magic potions and drugs.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fruit the Spirit produces is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control — and no law forbids such things. These are not achievements to manufacture but the character of Christ that the Spirit grows in believers.

Fruit, not works. The flesh has works; the Spirit has fruit. Works are manufactured — you decide, exert, produce. Fruit is grown by something the branch doesn’t do. No apple tree ever strained to produce an apple. And it is singular — one fruit with nine facets, not nine badges to collect. A single character, finally the character of Christ being formed in a person. You don’t pick patience this year and gentleness next; they come together because they are one life.

Love, joy, peace. Love heads the list, since the whole law is fulfilled in it (v. 14). Joy is not cheerful temperament; it survives circumstances that ruin cheerfulness, because its ground is outside them. Peace is first with God, and then the inward quiet of a man who has stopped negotiating his standing.

Toward others. Patience is “long-tempered” — a long fuse with people, the word used of God’s forbearance with us. Kindness is not politeness but active usefulness to someone. Goodness is moral substance: the same when nobody is checking.

Holding it together. Faithfulness: being reliable, where you said you would be. Gentleness: not weakness but strength under control, a word used of a powerful horse broken to the bridle. Self-control, last — striking on a list of what the Spirit produces, since every self-help programme sells it. Paul says it is a fruit. You don’t generate it; you receive it, then use it.

“Against such things there is no law.” Dry understatement that lands the chapter. The troublers feared grace would produce lawlessness. Paul says: look at what the Spirit produces, and find a legislature that would forbid any of it. The law was always aiming at this, and the Spirit produces it without the law’s help.

How is the fruit of the Spirit different from the gifts of the Spirit? The fruit is character, the same in every believer and growing for a lifetime. The gifts are abilities for service, distributed differently, “to each one individually as he wills” (1 Cor 12:11). The fruit matters more. Paul says that without love the greatest gifts are nothing (1 Cor 13:2), and Jesus warns of people who prophesied and cast out demons in his name and were never his (Matt 7:22–23). A church should prize holiness above gifting.

For the discouraged. A believer reads nine words, recognises few in himself, and concludes he has no Spirit. Three things. Fruit is slow and seasonal; nobody digs up a tree in March to check. You are the worst-placed person to assess it; ask the people who live with you, who usually report growth you can’t see. And the sentence doesn’t say “the fruit of the diligent Christian” but “of the Spirit” — and he is neither slow nor uncertain of the outcome. The growing was never your department. Stay close to him: in the Word, in prayer, among his people.
verseByVerse.note: “Fruit” is singular: one harvest with many flavours.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. It happened when they were united to Christ in his death. The old nature is condemned and dying, even though it is still loud.

Past tense. “Have crucified” — complete. Paul isn’t issuing an instruction here; he states what happened to every Christian, a fact before it is a duty.

Then what is fighting? Seven verses earlier Paul described a war inside the believer. If the flesh is dead, what has been fighting? The image answers it. Crucifixion wasn’t quick; Rome chose it because a man nailed to a beam could take days to die, mortally wounded, fixed in place, going nowhere — and still able to shout. He was finished, not yet silent. That is the flesh in a believer. Its authority is broken and its outcome settled, but it is still audible, and will be until the body dies. The voice you hear on a bad Thursday is real and loud, and it isn’t evidence that nothing happened to you. It is the noise of something executed that hasn’t yet stopped.

When? “I have been crucified with Christ” (2:20). At the cross, made yours when you were united to him (Romans 6:6). That is why the sentence begins “those who belong to Christ Jesus” — not unusually consecrated believers, but everyone who is his.

Relief in the order. If crucifying the flesh were your project, every failure would mean the work wasn’t done and must be restarted, and the Christian life would be a series of restarts. Because it is Christ’s finished work applied to you, your failures are the noise of a dying man, not the recovery of a victor. You aren’t trying to kill the flesh. You are refusing to take orders from something already condemned (Romans 8:13; Colossians 3:5). When the old voice speaks today, answer: you have no authority here; you were crucified with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit. Because the Spirit has given us life, we are to live in line with him — not running ahead in our own strength, nor lagging behind what he shows us.

“If” — meaning since. The Greek assumes it is true. Paul argues from fact to consequence, the shape of all New Testament ethics: this is what you are; be it. He never asks a Christian to become something to qualify.

Keep in step. In v. 16 the word was “walk.” Here it is a military term for keeping rank — marching in line, matching the step of the man beside you. And it shares the root of the “elementary principles” that enslaved the Galatians (4:3, 9). Paul takes the word for what held them in bondage and turns it into the word for walking free with the Spirit. They had marched before, to a calendar and a code. He doesn’t tell them to stop marching; he tells them who sets the pace now.

A different formation. Christian freedom isn’t the absence of order. Under the law you kept step with a system that couldn’t help you keep it; now with a Person who is himself the power to do it. Under the law the marching earned your standing; now it is what your standing produces (Romans 8:4).

Two ways to be out of step. You can march ahead — running on your own energy, taking initiatives you were never given, driving a ministry or decision at a pace nothing has been given to sustain, and calling the exhaustion faithfulness. Or you can lag behind — hearing the small thing you should do, agreeing with it, not doing it, until agreeing has replaced doing. Neither looks like rebellion. The correction is the same: find where he actually is, and be there. He sets a pace a real person can sustain over a whole life, which the law never did. A test: is there something you are rushing ahead with, or something you have agreed to and not done? Adjust your step this week.
verseByVerse.note: “Keep in step” is a military word for marching in line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not become conceited, provoking one another and envying one another. Walking with the Spirit shows itself in how we treat other believers. Pride and comparison destroy the fruit of the Spirit.

The hinge. This small verse stands between the fruit of the Spirit and chapter 6’s instructions on restoring a fallen brother. It brings the chapter’s soaring argument down onto how you feel about the Christian three seats away.

Empty glory. “Conceited” means empty-glory — a reputation held up by air. The moment a man’s significance rests on something that hollow, he can’t leave others alone, because a comparative standing can only be maintained comparatively.

Two symptoms, one disease. Provoking is what the man ahead does: needling, making sure the gap is felt. Envying is what the man behind does: resenting, watching, quietly hoping for a stumble. They look opposite and are identical: a person whose eyes are on another believer rather than Christ, calculating himself from the difference. That is what a religion of performance manufactures. If standing is earned, every other Christian is a rival or a reassurance. Only when a man knows he was received with empty hands do another man’s gifts stop being a threat.

A test. Think of the believer whose ministry, family or reputation is flourishing most visibly in your circle. What happens in you when his good news is announced? A flicker before the congratulation catches up is not a trivial temperament flaw. It is verse 26 with your name on it, placed right after the fruit of the Spirit because envy cannot coexist with love, joy and peace; it needs someone else to have less.

The cure. Not trying harder to be pleased, but looking elsewhere. Empty glory is attractive only while it is the best glory in view. Set beside the real thing — the Son of God who had glory in full, laid it down, “taking the form of a servant,” and was executed for people arguing about rank (Philippians 2:3–7) — the competition in the third row loses its grip. Pray today for the person you envy, by name, and thank God for what he has given them (John 3:30).
