6.title: Boasting Only in the Cross: The New Creation and the Community of Grace
6.overview:
The letter’s final chapter moves from the Spirit’s inner work to its outward expression in the community of faith. The freedom of the gospel, Paul has shown, is not moral permissiveness; it is the freedom that produces love, and love expresses itself in the concrete practices of the community. Chapter 6 describes what the community shaped by the gospel looks like: it bears burdens, restores the fallen gently, gives generously, sows to the Spirit, and refuses to grow weary in doing good.

The chapter reaches its climax in Paul’s autographic conclusion (vv. 11–18), where he returns one final time to the contrast that has driven the entire letter. The Judaizers boast in their circumcision program; they want to make a good showing in the flesh, to avoid persecution for the cross. Paul boasts in nothing except the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ — the event that crucified the world to him and him to the world. And this cross has created something radically new: not merely reformed Judaism, not a hybrid of law and grace, but a new creation. In the new creation, “neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.” The old categories — the categories by which the Judaizers were demanding conformity — have been abolished. What remains is the new creation in Christ, the Israel of God, the community of those who walk by the rule of the cross.

The letter ends as it began: with the gospel. Paul opened with grace and peace; he closes with “grace be with your spirit, brothers.” He opened with astonishment that they were deserting grace; he closes with the reminder that grace is still there, still sufficient, still the only ground on which any person, anywhere, stands before God. Galatians is, from first to last, a letter about grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul takes six chapters of doctrine and puts them to work on the hardest situation in ordinary church life. A brother caught in any transgression is to be restored — the word for mending a net or setting a bone — in a spirit of gentleness, by people who keep watch on themselves (v. 1). Verse 2 calls this bearing one another’s burdens and so fulfilling the law of Christ, which Paul has already defined as love (5:14). Verses 3–5 explain why restoration goes wrong: self-deception (v. 3), a verdict reached by comparison (v. 4), and forgetting that each will carry his own load on the day of account (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as a Community of Restoration

The Reformed tradition has never regarded the church as merely a preaching station but as a communion of saints — a body committed to mutual care, discipline and restoration. Verse 1 is the practical expression of the justification theology of the whole letter. We deal gently with a failing brother because we know we stand only by grace; the man who forgets his own proneness to sin will always be a prosecutor, and the man who remembers it will be a restorer. Gentleness without truth produces sentimentality, and truth without gentleness produces further fracture. Both are failures of the same verse.

Verses 2 and 5 together give the balance that keeps a church healthy, and both errors are recognisable. What is crushing a man, others are commanded to help carry; what is properly his own — his obedience, his repentance, his answer at the last day — nobody can carry for him, and pretending otherwise is not kindness. There is the Christian who will not let anyone near a weight that is breaking him and calls it strength, and the Christian who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church or his spouse and calls it fellowship.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatian congregations were biting and devouring one another (5:15). Freedom had evidently been taken by some as licence, and the response of others was condemnation rather than restoration. Verse 1 corrects both errors at once, and v. 3 names what was fuelling the second: men who thought they were something. Verse 4 answers the comparison culture that ends chapter 5 in provoking and envying.

Now:Verse 2 puts a question that a warm and orthodox church can still fail: whose weight are you actually under — not whom you pray for, which costs very little, but whose burden has cost you a Saturday or money you had other plans for? And v. 4 is uncomfortably clarifying: when you last felt good about your Christian life, was that a judgement about your work or about somebody else’s?

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a believer is caught in a sin, those who are walking by the Spirit should restore him gently — and watch themselves, so that they are not tempted too. Paul puts his doctrine to work on the hardest situation in church life: what to do about a Christian who has fallen.

Caught. The verb is passive: overtaken, caught out, ambushed. Not a man who planned his rebellion but one walking along and surprised. That doesn’t make the sin smaller — Paul calls it a transgression, a false step — but it changes your posture. You are looking at a casualty, not a defector.

“You who are spiritual.” Not an elite tier; every Christian lives by the Spirit (5:25). The spiritual are those actually keeping in step with him today. And there is an edge: the Galatians were full of people who thought themselves advanced. If you are so spiritual, here is the job.

Restore. The word is used of mending torn nets (Matthew 4:21) and of setting a broken bone. Nobody sets a bone carelessly or by shouting at it. You must get close, know what you are doing, cause pain deliberately and only as much as the job needs — and the whole aim is a limb that works again. A surgeon who enjoyed the pain would be struck off.

Gentleness. The word from the fruit of the Spirit four verses earlier (5:23). Paul has said what the Spirit produces; now he shows where it is needed most. Gentleness isn’t softness about the sin; it is strength under control.

“Keep watch on yourself.” Suddenly singular, spoken to the one doing the restoring. The danger is rarely committing the same sin. It is enjoying the position — finding that being the one who is well is unexpectedly pleasant, relaying the details as a “prayer request,” feeling firm ground under you that wasn’t there last week. That is worse than what you came to mend, and invisible to the man in it (1 Corinthians 10:12).

How to do it. Go to him, rather than discussing him. Ask first whether you would want this conversation conducted on you the way you are about to conduct it. Say the true thing plainly; gentleness that won’t name the sin is cowardice wearing its coat. And go knowing that only grace you didn’t generate separates you from him. A man who has grasped the first five chapters of this letter can’t be a prosecutor; he has read the charge sheet with his own name on it.

And if the person will not be restored? Then the gentleness does not give way to indifference. Jesus lays out the steps: go privately, then with one or two others, then to the church (Matt 18:15–17). Where someone who calls himself a believer persists in serious sin without repentance, the church must act (1 Cor 5:11–13), always with the aim of bringing him back (James 5:19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” Christians are to carry the crushing weights others cannot carry alone. That is the law of Christ: to love one another as he loved us — he who carried our burden to the cross.

Heavy loads. “Bear” means go on carrying, as a habit, and “burdens” are crushing weights — not minor inconveniences but things genuinely too much for one person: a failing marriage, a diagnosis, a son who has stopped speaking, the sin from v. 1 a man can’t get free of alone. And verses 1 and 2 belong together. Dealing with someone’s sin, done as v. 1 describes, is bearing his burden.

The law of Christ. Paul has spent five chapters saying believers are not under law, and now uses the word positively with Christ’s name on it. He isn’t smuggling the old system back in. He has already said what it is: “the whole law is fulfilled in one word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (5:14). And Jesus gave it as “a new commandment… that you love one another: just as I have loved you” (John 13:34). The law of Christ is the law of love, defined by a life rather than a list — and the standard is no longer “as yourself” but “as I have loved you,” which is far more expensive.

His name on it. Christ didn’t only legislate burden-bearing. He bore the burden no one else could: “Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4). When a Christian takes the weight of another’s failure onto his shoulders, he does in miniature, at infinite distance, what was done for him at Calvary.

A test. Whose weight are you under right now? Not whom do you pray for — prayer costs a Christian little and can be done entirely in his own house. Whose burden has cost you a Saturday, money you had other plans for, or a friendship that grew harder because you told the truth in it? A church can be doctrinally immaculate, warm on Sunday, and carrying nothing at all, because burden-bearing is invisible and voluntary and nobody notices its absence. Pick up someone’s burden this week.

Not reciprocal on any given Tuesday. “One another’s”: over years in a healthy church it evens out. But not week by week, and the man who keeps accounts won’t last. You carry, and sometimes you are carried, and the ledger between you was closed at the cross (Romans 15:1).

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will have to bear his own load.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who thinks he is something when he is nothing deceives himself. Each should test his own work instead of comparing himself with others. For while we help carry each other’s crushing burdens, each must carry his own load — his own obedience and his own account before God.

Self-assessment. These verses explain why restoration goes wrong: not technique but self-assessment. “If anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself” — leads his own mind astray. Spiritual pride is the one sin that blinds you specifically to itself. A man knows when he has lost his temper. Nobody has ever thought, “This morning I am inflated.”

“Nothing.” Not worthless — Paul has spent two chapters calling them sons and heirs. Nothing on your own account. Everything worth having came as a gift, and a man who forgets that has mistaken a delivery for an achievement.

Test your own work. The verb is for assaying metal — putting it in the fire to find what it is rather than what it looks like. And the object is “his own work.” The Galatians were measuring themselves against each other (5:26). A man who has assayed his own work has a real, modest sense of what God gave him to do and whether he is doing it. A man who measures against his neighbour has nothing, because his verdict depends on who is standing next to him and changes when the neighbour changes.

A test. When you last felt good about your Christian life, was that a judgment about your work or someone else’s? And when you last felt a failure? For most people, most of both feelings is arithmetic performed on other people. This week, measure yourself against God’s word and calling, not against a brother.

Burden and load. Verse 5 seems to contradict v. 2: bear one another’s burdens; each must bear his own load. Two things resolve it. The words differ. Verse 2’s “burdens” are crushing weights. Verse 5’s “load” is a soldier’s pack or a ship’s cargo — an assignment proportioned to the carrier, the word in “my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). And the tense differs: v. 2 is about now; v. 5 is future, “will have to bear,” looking to the day each gives his own account, where no one can stand in the queue for us.

Two errors. What crushes you, others are commanded to help carry. What is properly yours — your obedience, your repentance, your answer at the last day — nobody can carry, and it isn’t kind to pretend otherwise. There is the Christian who won’t let anyone near a weight that is breaking him, and calls it strength. And there is the one who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church, counsellor or spouse, and calls it fellowship. Which are you more prone to?
verseByVerse.note: A “burden” in verse 2 is a crushing weight; a “load” in verse 5 is one’s own pack.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6 arrives without preliminaries and it is about money: let the one taught share all good things with the one who teaches. The verb is koinōneitō, from the word for fellowship, which tells you Paul did not regard the subject as a lower order of thing. Note also who is instructed — congregations to give, not teachers to raise support. The reversal has done real damage, because a man who must ask for his own living finds it very hard to say the unwelcome thing, and this letter exists because somebody said one.

Verse 7 hardens the tone. God is not mocked uses a verb built on the word for the nose: nobody sneers at God and gets away with it. The farming principle that follows carries three certainties every agricultural town understood — you reap what you sowed, more than you sowed, and later than you sowed. It is the third that deceives people, because the gap is long enough to make the connection look unreal. Verse 8 names the two fields, and corruption is phthoran, decay: the flesh pays out not usually in catastrophe but in decomposition. The promise of eternal life to those who sow to the Spirit is not wages — six chapters forbid that — but the full growth of a life that was given.

Verse 9 assumes weariness rather than forbidding it, and Paul includes himself in the us. The one condition attached to the harvest is not achievement but persistence: if we do not give up. Verse 10 turns the weariness outward. As we have opportunity uses the same word as the season in v. 9, so the sowing season is now — which disposes of the commonest evasion, since it means while there is time, not when it is convenient. Doing good to everyone forbids the church turned inward; especially to the household of faith forbids a general benevolence that never reaches the believer two streets away.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest as the Motive of Present Faithfulness

Reformed ethics has always read present obedience in the light of a future harvest, and vv. 7–9 are where Paul states it most plainly. The believer does not do good in order to earn the harvest; the harvest is secured by grace, and this letter has spent six chapters proving that nothing a man sows can purchase eternal life. But the harvest is real and the reaping is certain, and the knowledge of it sustains present faithfulness. That is the farmer’s wisdom applied to the Christian life, not works-righteousness.

Verse 8 must be read in the terms already set, or it will contradict the letter. What it describes is a direction of life: the seed a man scatters shows which field he believes he lives in, and a person indwelt by the Spirit sows to the Spirit for the same reason a living tree puts out leaves. And v. 6 grounds the support of gospel ministry in something older than church order — the Levites had no land and Israel ate with them, and Paul states the principle elsewhere as the labourer deserving his wages (1 Cor. 9:11; 1 Tim. 5:17–18), which is the Lord’s own saying.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were weary — theologically confused, socially fragmented, and without Paul. The Judaizers’ programme was more structured and far more socially comfortable, and drifting toward it would have ended the trouble. Verse 9 is aimed exactly there: the harvest is coming, do not walk off the field. And v. 6 was not incidental either, since nothing in a congregation's life is a more exact readout of what its people actually believe than what happens to their money.

Now:Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable, which is why v. 8 so rarely frightens anyone into faithfulness; and v. 9 belongs to named people at the end of their strength, to whom Paul offers not encouragement about their prospects but a fact about the universe.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are taught God’s word should share all good things with their teacher. Supporting those who teach the Scriptures is a form of fellowship — and a direct test of what a congregation really values.

Sharing is fellowship. “Share” is from the family of koinōnia, fellowship — the New Testament’s word for the deepest communion of the church. Paul uses it of paying the teacher, so he didn’t regard money as a lower subject. Money is fellowship in its most testable form. And “all good things” is broad: not only money but food, hospitality, the ordinary things a household can share.

The congregation gives. Paul doesn’t tell teachers to raise support; he tells congregations to give it. That is the healthy direction. A man who must ask for his own living finds it hard to say the unwelcome thing — and this letter exists because someone said a very unwelcome thing.

Consistent teaching. “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you?” (1 Corinthians 9:11). “The laborer deserves his wages” (1 Timothy 5:18), quoting Jesus. The Levites had no land, and Israel shared with them. And it comes here, right before “God is not mocked… whatever one sows, that will he also reap” — whose first application is what a congregation does with its money.

Paul’s own freedom. Paul sometimes refused support, making tents in Corinth rather than be a burden (1 Corinthians 9:15–18). So paid ministry isn’t the only faithful shape. But this is an instruction to the congregation, which may not use the apostle’s freedom as an excuse. He chose to go without; he never said the teacher wasn’t owed.

A test. What is your giving decided by? Many Christians give from what is left, so the teaching of the word is funded by the residue of a lifestyle designed without reference to it. Paul’s word is “share” — not tip, subsidise, or fund from surplus. It assumes a common life in which what one has is available to the other, a more disturbing idea than a percentage. Decide this week what you will share with those who teach you, before you spend the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap.” A life spent sowing to the sinful nature reaps decay; a life sown to the Spirit reaps eternal life. God’s moral order cannot be outwitted, however long the harvest takes.

Not mocked. “Mocked” is from the word for the nose: to turn your nose up, to sneer. God doesn’t get sneered at — not that he takes offence, but that nobody gets away with it. You may treat him as a system to be worked around; the treatment doesn’t succeed.

Three certainties of the farm. You reap what you sow: no farmer is surprised by the species of his crop. You reap more than you sow: a handful of seed returns a sheaf, both ways. And you reap later than you sow — the certainty that deceives people, because the gap is long enough to make the connection seem unreal. That gap is what v. 7 aims at. Nobody sneers at God during harvest. The sneer comes in month four, when nothing has followed and the warning seems overwrought. Paul’s answer isn’t that judgment comes quickly but that the ground keeps the account whether anyone is watching.

Corruption. “Sows to his own flesh will… reap corruption” — decay, rotting. A precise description, not just a threat. The flesh pays out less in catastrophe than in decomposition: a marriage quietly gone hollow, an appetite needing more each year to do the same work, a conscience that stops registering, a man in his sixties who can’t say what he built. Nothing dramatic happened. It simply went off.

Not wages. “The one who sows to the Spirit will… reap eternal life.” This can sound like wages for services, which would contradict the whole letter. Eternal life is God’s gift in Christ (Romans 6:23), and this letter spends six chapters proving nothing you sow can buy it. Verse 8 describes a direction of life. The seed a man scatters shows which field he thinks he lives in, and someone indwelt by the Spirit sows to the Spirit as a living tree puts out leaves. The harvest isn’t his wages; it is the full growth of a life given to him (Romans 8:13).

Small seeds. Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable; nobody sows a field in an afternoon. This morning’s twenty minutes with the Bible open, the apology you made instead of the point you were entitled to, the money given quietly, the conversation with the difficult person at church — none felt like anything. That is what seed is like in the hand. Christians seldom connect their spiritual dullness to anything because they look for a cause the size of the effect, and there never is one. There is a field, and what has gone into it for eleven years. What will you sow today?

Is this karma? No. Karma is an impersonal law of cause and effect that no one can escape. Here a personal God is speaking, who forgives, and who laid the penalty of his people’s sin on Christ. But forgiveness does not always remove the earthly consequences of sin. David was forgiven, “The LORD also has put away your sin,” and yet the child died (2 Sam 12:13–14); and God disciplines those he loves (Heb 12:6). Nor does every hardship mean a person is reaping a particular sin; Job and the man born blind (John 9:3) show otherwise. What this verse warns against is thinking we can sow to the flesh and escape the harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.” So while we have opportunity, we should do good to everyone, and especially to fellow believers. The harvest comes in God’s time to those who keep going.

“Us.” After five chapters of “you,” Paul puts himself inside the exhortation. The apostle knew what it was to be tired of doing good.

Weariness assumed. He doesn’t tell them to stop being weary; he assumes it. The verb means losing heart, going slack, running out of will to continue — not wickedness but ordinary exhaustion. A Christian worn out from carrying burdens, restoring the fallen and giving money away isn’t in a state Paul finds surprising. He is in the state this verse was written for.

In due season. At its own proper time. No farmer resents June for not being September. He works a field that shows nothing for months, because the timetable was never his, and he knows the difference between “nothing is happening” and “nothing is visible.”

The one condition. “If we do not give up.” Not if we sow enough, well, or with the right motives — if we don’t stop. The risk here isn’t failure but abandonment: walking off the field in the eleventh year, three weeks before something comes up.

For the weary. The mother who has prayed for a son for twenty-two years and stopped expecting the phone to ring. The man teaching eight children in a back room while the church around him talks about growth. The wife who has been gentle with a hard husband for a decade with nothing to show. The small-town pastor who has buried more than he has baptised. Paul’s answer isn’t encouragement about prospects but a fact about the universe: sowing is followed by reaping, and the season is God’s. Don’t stop this week (1 Corinthians 15:58).

While there is opportunity. “As we have opportunity” uses the same word as “season.” The harvest has its season, and so does the sowing, and the sowing season is now. That disposes of the commonest evasion: “as we have opportunity” doesn’t mean “when convenient” but “while there is still time.”

Everyone, and especially the household. Both halves correct a failure. “Everyone” forbids the church turned inward, doing good only where it will be appreciated by people who share its views. “Especially” forbids the sentimentality that treats general goodwill toward mankind as a substitute for helping the believer two streets away whose boiler has failed. Family first, not family only — and a family runs no application process. The claim on you isn’t that he deserves it but that he is kin. Who in your church needs practical help this week?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — The Cross and the New Creation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
In v. 11 Paul takes the pen from his secretary and writes the closing paragraph himself, in large letters — the ancient equivalent of underlining hard enough to score the page. What he writes large is not doctrine but motive. Verse 12 says the men forcing circumcision want to make a good showing in the flesh and to avoid persecution for the cross, which had a concrete meaning in that century: Judaism was a recognised religion under Rome, and circumcised converts made the whole problem disappear for everyone. Verse 13 exposes the second motive, converts as trophies, and adds the detail that collapses the programme — the men selling the law do not keep it themselves, which 5:3 said it obligates them to.

Verse 14 answers with the sharpest contrast in the letter. They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows, and far be it from me is his most violent negative. The cross was not yet jewellery: it was Rome’s method for killing slaves in public, and for a Pharisee it carried the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23 that Paul quoted at 3:13. The double crucifixion he describes runs both ways — the world's offers have lost their force on him, and he has lost his standing in its eyes, which is the harder half and precisely what the Judaizers were avoiding.

Verse 15 gives the verdict: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, but a new creation — kainē ktisis, new in kind, the age to come arriving early in a person, not a renovation of the old. Verse 16 pronounces peace and mercy on all who walk by that rule, and on the Israel of God, the most argued-over phrase in the letter. Verse 17 closes the case not with an argument but with scars — stigmata, the brand of ownership — and v. 18 ends where 1:3 began, with grace, and with the word brothers standing last in the Greek sentence before the Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross as the Permanent Centre, and the Israel of God

Paul’s boast in v. 14 is the summary of everything the letter has argued. The cross is where the law’s curse was absorbed, where the old creation died and the new was born, and Reformed theology has always insisted it is not merely the entrance to the Christian life but its permanent centre — the ground the believer stands on at every moment from conversion to glory. This is Luther’s theology of the cross against a theology of glory: God’s ways are read from below, through shame and suffering, not from above through human notions of power and success.

On v. 16 everything turns on the small word kai, which can mean “and” or “even.” Read as “even the Israel of God,” the phrase caps the sentence: those who walk by this rule, Jew and Gentile together, are the Israel of God, which is the standard Reformed reading and is supported by 3:29 and 4:26. Read as simply “and,” a second group is in view, most naturally believing Jews. The first fits the letter’s whole argument best; the second is held by serious readers who love this book, including many who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11. On what actually matters here nobody disagrees: whoever they are, the rule they walk by is the cross and the new creation, and no one enters that number by ancestry or by a mark.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted social safety, and vv. 12–13 name it without charity: circumcising the Gentiles satisfied the synagogue and left Rome uninterested. Verse 17 answers it with the marks Paul carried from his sufferings, among them the stoning at Lystra in Galatia itself (Acts 14:19).

Now:The test v. 13 puts to a softened conviction is not whether the reason is defensible but what the adjustment costs you. And v. 17 belongs to anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something unglamorous — Paul filed his scars under the same heading as the wounds of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul takes the pen and writes in large letters with his own hand. The false teachers want to make a good impression and avoid persecution for the cross; they push circumcision so they can boast about it — though they don’t even keep the law themselves. Their real motive is safety and status.

Large letters. Letters were usually dictated, with the author adding a line in his own hand as a signature (2 Thessalonians 3:17). Here Paul takes over the whole closing paragraph and writes big — perhaps because of poor eyes (cf. 4:15), chiefly for emphasis, like underlining hard enough to score the page. What follows is the whole letter compressed, and he doesn’t want it missed.

Motive. What he writes large is not doctrine but motive. “Those who want to make a good showing in the flesh” — literally, to present a fine face, to look good in public. And what they buy with the Galatians’ circumcision: “only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.”

The pressure behind it. Judaism had legal recognition and exemptions under Rome. A movement of circumcised Jews following a Messiah could shelter under that. A movement of uncircumcised Gentiles worshipping a crucified Jew couldn’t; it looked like apostasy to the synagogue and an unlicensed sect to Rome. Meanwhile Jewish nationalism was rising, and Jewish Christians seen dissolving the boundary paid for it at home. So the troublers were men under pressure doing something understandable: get the Gentiles circumcised and the problem vanishes. Any reasonable committee might reach that solution.

Trophies. “That they may boast in your flesh.” Converts as trophies — something done to another man’s body that can be counted and reported. Every generation of ministry has its version: the number, the testimony repeated at conferences, the person who has become a credential.

They don’t keep it either. Circumcision obligates a man to the whole law (5:3), and the men selling it aren’t keeping it. So it was never a serious attempt at law-righteousness. It was a way of belonging safely, dressed in Scripture.

A test. If you have ever softened a Christian conviction and given a theological reason for it, the test isn’t whether your reason is defensible; the troublers had excellent reasons, one of which was avoiding a beating. The test is what the adjustment costs you. Every change they proposed made their lives easier, and the flesh has never recommended a course that would get its owner persecuted. Paul’s alternative, in the next verse, is a cross — exactly what the whole manoeuvre was designed to avoid. Is there a conviction you have quietly softened to stay comfortable? Take it back up.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then took the pen himself to finish; his large letters may reflect poor eyesight or simply emphasis.

verseByVerse.quote: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will boast in nothing except “the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” The cross is his only ground of glory, and it has broken the world’s hold on him and his standing in it.

A gallows to boast in. They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows. “Far be it from me” is his strongest negative: the thought of boasting in anything else is unthinkable.

How strange it sounded. The cross wasn’t yet jewellery. It was Rome’s instrument for killing slaves and rebels in public, so shameful that polite writers avoided the word; Cicero said the very name should be far from a Roman citizen. And a Pharisee knew Deuteronomy 21:23, quoted at 3:13: “a hanged man is cursed by God.” To boast in a crucifixion was blasphemy to a Jew and disgusting to a Roman. That is the one thing Paul will glory in — not his spectacular conversion, unmatched missionary record, learning, visions or suffering, but something done for him rather than by him (1 Corinthians 2:2).

A double death. “The world has been crucified to me”: its offers have lost their force. Standing, security, the approval you were raised to want aren’t evil, and Paul doesn’t despise them; they are dead to him. They can’t buy him, because he has seen what they had no answer for. “And I to the world”: he has lost his standing in its eyes too — the harder half, the one the troublers were desperate to avoid. A man dead to the world is one the world has finished assessing. He isn’t ranked, because he isn’t a candidate. That is why he was free to write this letter and they were not.

In an ordinary life. With a mortgage and a family, it isn’t withdrawal. Paul had a trade, travelled, and cared about money for the poor. It means the world can still take things from you but can no longer take anything that matters, and can no longer set your price.

A test. What would happen if the reputation you have built quietly collapsed — not through sin, just being overlooked or misunderstood? If you would lose something painful but survivable, the crucifixion has been done. If you wouldn’t know who you were, the world is still very much alive. Look today at the Son of God on a beam outside the city, numbered with criminals, bearing a curse that belonged to others — the universe’s one boast — and let it set your price.

verseByVerse.quote: For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is “a new creation.” Peace and mercy rest on all who live by this rule, and on “the Israel of God.” What matters is not a mark on the body but whether God has made a person new.

Three endings to one sentence. In 5:6 what counts is “faith working through love”; in 1 Corinthians 7:19, “keeping the commandments of God”; here, “a new creation.” One point: never the mark on the body, always whether God has done something.

New creation. “New” means new in kind, not just recent. Paul reaches back to Genesis 1 and forward to Isaiah’s new heavens and earth. The gospel doesn’t produce a reformed version of the old — a better man, a tidied religion, Judaism with the hard parts adjusted. It is the age to come arriving early, in a person: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). That is why the troublers’ offer was hopeless. They proposed an alteration to someone already raised — the difference between renovating a house and being born.

The rule. “All who walk by this rule” — a measuring rod: not circumcision, not uncircumcision, but new creation. “Peace and mercy” — Paul’s usual greeting is grace and peace; here mercy comes second, as though at the end of a severe letter he wants the last word on the Galatians to be that they will be dealt with kindly.

“The Israel of God.” The most argued-over phrase in the letter. Everything turns on a small word that can mean “and” or “even.” Read “even the Israel of God,” and those who walk by this rule — Jew and Gentile in Christ — are the Israel of God. That is the standard Reformed reading, and the letter supports it: those who are Christ’s are “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (3:29), and “the Jerusalem above… is our mother” (4:26). Read “and,” and a second group is in view, most naturally Jewish believers, singled out for blessing at the end of a letter hard on their nation’s badge. The first is more persuasive, because it is what six chapters argue. But the second is held by careful readers who love this book, many expecting a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11. On what matters here, nobody disagrees: whoever the Israel of God is, peace and mercy rest on them, and the rule they walk by is the cross and new creation. No one gets into that number by ancestry or a mark.

No papers checked. The Galatians had been told for months that they were outsiders, provincial latecomers, always second-tier. Paul’s final blessing lays peace and mercy on everyone walking by this rule and checks nobody’s papers. A test: what do you look to as the sign that you belong to God — a mark, a heritage, a church — or a heart God has made new? Thank him for the new creation he has begun in you.
verseByVerse.note: Interpreters differ over whether “the Israel of God” means believing Jews or the whole church, Jew and Gentile together. The more persuasive reading is the whole church (compare 3:29).

verseByVerse.quote: From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on, let no one trouble Paul: he bears on his body “the marks of Jesus” — the scars of suffering for Christ. He ends where he began, with grace: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.”

The marks. The word is stigmata: a brand burned or cut into a slave to show whose he was, a soldier to show whose army, a temple servant to show whose god. Set that against the letter. The troublers wanted a mark cut into Gentile flesh to prove belonging. Paul says: I have marks, unchosen and put there by people trying to stop me — the rods at Philippi (Acts 16:22), the stones at Lystra in Galatia itself, where some hearing this letter may have watched him dragged out and left for dead (Acts 14:19; 2 Corinthians 11:23–25). Those are his credentials, and they settle whose he is far more conclusively than circumcision.

“From now on.” The case is closed. After six chapters of covenants, chronology, Abraham, Hagar and the Spirit, he simply shows the scars.

For the scarred. If your faithfulness has cost you something visible and unglamorous — a career that went nowhere because of a conviction, a family that cooled, a body worn out in a small work nobody counted — those marks are not evidence that you managed life badly. Paul filed his under the same heading as the wounds of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:10) and expected them to be honoured. Don’t be ashamed of them.

The last word. Not “foolish Galatians,” not a warning, not an opponent’s name. In Greek the sentence ends, just before the Amen, with “brothers.” The man who wrote an anathema in chapter 1 signs off calling them family.

Grace at both ends. He began with grace (1:3) and ends with grace, and everything between argues that nothing may be added to it — not circumcision, a calendar, Jerusalem’s endorsement, or the record of the person reading this. A Son sent in the fullness of time, born of woman, born under the law, who kept it and then was made a curse on a tree so the blessing sworn to Abraham could reach a farmer in Lystra with nothing to bring; who bought slaves out of the market, gave them his name, put his Spirit in their hearts and taught them to say “Father.” Nothing was cheapened; everything was paid; all of it was grace. Live today on nothing but that grace. Amen.
verseByVerse.note: The “marks” were the scars left by beatings and stoning — like the brands on a slave showing whom he belonged to.
